item.title: Dan Campbell credits Mike Kafka for big play to Amon-Ra St. Brown
item.description: The Lions ran what may have been the most inventive play of the week in the NFL when wide receiver Amon-Ra St.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions ran what may have been the most inventive play of the week in the NFL when wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown lined up 15 yards behind the line of scrimmage and got a running start of about 10 yards before Jared Goff threw him the ball, meaning that St. Brown was at full speed by the time the Vikings' defense had a chance to touch him. St. Brown gained 10 yards on the play.

Lions head coach Dan Campbell said on 97.1 The Ticket that Lions passing game coordinator Mike Kafka came up with that play.

"That was Kafka's baby. Like most plays, somebody gets an idea, and then you start massaging it, you slap it against the wall, 'What about this?' and everyone picks away at it," Campbell said. "We all have ideas and you throw them against the wall and it's either perfect or you start massaging it a little bit, you start tinkering. But that one started from Kafka, it was awesome. We'd had it up a couple weeks, just hadn't run it yet, and this was a good week to do it."

It was a great time to do it, and now the Lions' upcoming opponents have something unique they have to be prepared for.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings for Week 9: Are they beginning to Bo-lieve?
item.description: The national media has to start taking notice of the 6-2 Denver Broncos. They don’t quite bo-lieve yet, but if they keep winning….
item.content:encoded:
Four straight wins and sitting in the number two seed in the AFC. That’s where the Denver Broncos are heading into Week 9, which means the national media has to start paying attention and most did in their power rankings this week.

If I had to be honest with where each team is at in the NFL, I would probably put the Broncos somewhere around 4th and 5th right now. I think the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, Chicago Bears are all playing more complete football right now. From there, you could split hairs between our Broncos and teams like the Detroit Lions and Jacksonville Jaguars.

If Denver keeps winning, however, they’ll continue be harder and harder to ignore. The media will be forced to start bo-lieving in this football team team.

Here’s how the Broncos are doing in this week’s power rankings around the web:

NFL.com – 6th

Denver recorded a huge win over the Chiefs with a frantic fourth-quarter comeback that should give Broncos fans hope the team can climb out of its offensive struggles before long. There were signs that it’s starting to turn for the better: Bo Nix pushed the ball downfield successfully a few times, Jonah Coleman broke out in a fashion that usually leads to an increase in importance, and the defense once again finished the job. If the Broncos can follow this trajectory, they’ll round into top form by December — and thanks to Sunday’s triumph, they’ll be right in the thick of the race for the AFC West crown.

NBC Sports – 4th

They out-chiefed the Chiefs.

ESPN – 4th

The Broncos acquired Hall of Famer Gary Zimmerman just before the start of the 1993 regular season, so the wayback machine had to be fired up to get to the best in-season trade. The Broncos acquired Moses from the Bills via a one-for-one swap for Dwight Harrison. Moses played nine full seasons for the Broncos after the 1972 season, averaging at least 17 yards a catch in eight of those years and having 44 total touchdown catches. He is in the team’s Ring of Fame and played on the franchise’s first Super Bowl team in 1977.

Yahoo Sports – 9th

The idea that the Broncos could make a big move for Jonathan Taylor is dubious only because Sean Payton’s history of using committees at running back without a standout workhorse. And the team has to be intrigued by rookie Jonah Coleman, who has played well and came up with two big plays to give Denver the lead in a huge win over the Chiefs on Sunday.

Perhaps Taylor or another big-time back could solve some issues on the offense. Or maybe it’s a receiver or a tight end, after the Evan Engram signing in 2025 has been a dud. Even some depth on the offensive line isn’t a bad idea. The Broncos are set on defense, so their focus can be how to add an impact piece to an inconsistent offense.

USA Today – 3rd

If they don’t have your respect yet, then how about this nugget – they’ve won five consecutive home games against former league MVPs. This 6-2 squad has also survived the most brutal stretch of its schedule and is set up to coast to another AFC West crown if it can take care of business.

Fox Sports – 2nd

I’ve still got my worries about Bo Nix. At some point, the Broncos are going to need a lot more from him. But he’s doing enough right now, especially for a team that can’t run the ball effectively. He makes enough big plays — though usually they are short passes that someone turns into a big play — and doesn’t make many big mistakes. In fact, he’s gone five straight games without an interception. With a coach like Sean Payton and a defense playing as well as the Broncos’ is, that’s more than enough. For now.

CBS Sports – 5th

They have a lot of late-game magic to win games. That formula has worked for this team, but for how long?

NY Times – 3rd

The rookie running back led Denver in rushing (41) and receiving (63) yards on Sunday and is a delight to watch, but the hot rumor coming out of this game was that the Broncos might be in the Jonathan Taylor trade discussions. If that comes to fruition, the offense will be better, but we’ll miss Coleman.

What do you think of these power rankings? Share in the comments section below!

item.content:encoded:
Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season is nearly a wrap, with just the Chicago Bears and Seattle Seahawks left to play on "Monday Night Football."

There was plenty of excitement on Sunday, including two games that went into overtime, but they unfortunately weren't without injuries. Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson made his return to the lineup after rehabbing an ankle injury, but that excitement was short-lived, as he suffered a thumb injury on his first pass attempt of the game. Per head coach Jesse Minter, he'll require surgery and a stint on the injured reserve list — a brutal blow.

Backup Tyler Huntley is also dealing with what is thought to be a turf toe injury, which forced Baltimore to resort to their emergency third quarterback, Joe Fagnano. He completed 10-of-21 passes for 91 yards and an interception in relief of Jackson and Huntley this week.

The Ravens are playing on a short week, as they're set to host the Jacksonville Jaguars on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 9.

The Detroit Lions handed the Minnesota Vikings their first loss of the season, but lost a key playmaker on defense as All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell suffered a scary-looking neck injury. He was immobilized on a backboard before being transported to the hospital as his teammates gathered around him in an emotional scene.

item.title: Broncos overtake Chiefs as favorites in AFC West
item.description: There's a new favorite to win the AFC West.
item.content:encoded:
There's a new favorite to win the AFC West.

After beating the Chiefs on Sunday and improving to 6-2 on the season, the Broncos are now the betting favorites to win the division, for the first time this season.

The Broncos' odds to win the division are at -130. The Chiefs are close behind at +115. The Raiders are very long shots at +2500 and the winless Chargers are extreme long shots at +15,000.

The Chiefs had spent this season as the favorites, especially after blowing out the Broncos in Week 1. But the Chiefs are now on a two-game losing streak, and at 5-2 a half game behind the Broncos in the division.

The AFC West looks like it's going to be a two-horse race that goes deep into the season. At the moment, it's the Broncos who have the edge.

item.title: Week 9 NFL Power Rankings: Trade Deadline Status and Needs for Each Team
item.description: Week 8 is in the books, and the trade deadline is right around the corner. Here’s each team's outlook and power ranking from @AaronLemingNFL.
item.content:encoded:
November is here, and the trade deadline is just six days away. With the playoff picture finally unfolding and the contenders separating themselves from the pretenders, things are expected to ramp up throughout the week. Even though we’ve already had multiple big trades, the reshaping of the league is far from over. Before we turn the page on Week 8, let’s take a look at each team’s deadline status and what fans can expect to happen in Week 9’s WCG NFL Power Rankings.

1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

Reports suggest the 49ers will be one of the more aggressive teams at the deadline, which makes sense given their hot start, previous injuries, and the window they’re in due to their roster age. They’ve already added DeForest Buckner, but a receiver is a sneaky need, especially considering the injuries, but don’t be surprised to see them add an interior offensive lineman. With Quenton Nelson heading to Seattle, Buckner was a great counter. Still, considering the age of their roster, they might want to add another impact player to be safe. 

2. Buffalo Bills (6-1)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

The Bills are contenders not only to win the division and make the playoffs but also to compete for a Super Bowl. Injuries at receiver have made that position look a little worse than expected, but with D.J. Moore back in the mix, that should improve. To get over the hump, the Bills need to add defensive talent, especially in the secondary. Either a cornerback or safety makes the most sense. Either way, they need to make a move. 

3. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

The Jaguars are in good shape to win the division and make it back to the playoffs, but some holes on this team could be filled through deadline acquisitions after a quiet offseason. Additions at receiver, cornerback, or along the offensive line would make sense, but we’ll see how much second-year general manager James Gladstone wants to spend. This is already a well-rounded team, but it’s fair to wonder whether it has enough to compete for a Super Bowl as is. 

4. Detroit Lions (5-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

The two years of dominance that we saw from the Lions with Ben Johnson and Aaron Glenn as star coordinators are gone. This offense is still damn good, but the defense has kept them from being truly elite. Detroit has a few key players to pay next offseason, but there should still be enough flexibility to add if needed. Cornerback stands out as a primary need, but depth at running back or on the defensive line could also make sense. 

5. Denver Broncos (6-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

Unfortunately for Denver, no quarterback upgrades will be available. Ok, I’m only (kind of) joking. That said, they need to figure out how to improve the offense. Jonathan Taylor has been a “big swing” type of name to come up at running back, but maybe another tight end could also make sense? The biggest issue is that few, if any, impact names are expected to be available. That, of course, assumes that the Lions don’t cut bait with Sam LaPorta early like they did with T.J. Hockenson a few years ago. 

6. Minnesota Vikings (6-1)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

Through seven weeks, the Vikings have been the surprise of the league. Although many believed they were better than their record last season, a 6-0 start wasn’t on anybody’s radar. They’ve been aggressive at the deadline, but who or what they target is the bigger question. They could use help on the interior offensive line, and some have speculated that running back Jonathan Taylor would make sense as a big splash. Never rule out a defensive addition with this group either. We’ll see what shakes out over the next week. 

7. Chicago Bears (6-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

Defense was a need going into the offseason, and it remained a need heading into the season. Despite playing better than expected, it made sense that Chicago was still an impact piece (or two) away from being considered a legitimate Super Bowl contender. Even after adding Jeffery Simmons, additional defensive line help or a starting-caliber cornerback should still be a priority. Another sneaky need: tight end depth, following the season-ending injury to Cole Kmet. 

8. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

Despite their hot start, the Chiefs have clear holes, especially on offense, that they’ll need to address if they expect a successful postseason run. Receiving is front and center as their biggest need, but don’t rule out a move along the offensive line, especially with Josh Simmons going to Injured Reserve and reportedly being kicked out of a meeting. General manager Brett Veach must be aggressive over the next week-plus. 

9. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

I’ve been saying this for years, but I’m not really sure what the long-term goals are for the Steelers; for now, they are a playoff contender. That said, they have one of the older rosters in the league, and not many gaping holes. In theory, they could stand to add a receiver, but Michael Pittman Jr. should be back soon. Considering this is the last year of Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers don’t look like a Super Bowl contender, I’m not sure trading away a valuable asset for a receiver makes sense. 

10. Green Bay Packers (5-3)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

Green Bay is in an interesting spot as we inch toward the deadline. Clearly, they have the talent to get back to the playoffs, but they are in a deep division, and most of their issues aren’t magically going to go away without action. The offensive line and interior defensive line need upgrades, and linebacker is another sneaky need because of the season-ending injury to Edgerrin Cooper. It’s hard to see them making a splash move as they are still recouping draft picks from the Micah Parsons deal, but parting with a Day 3 pick for some help is surely on the table. 

11. Cincinnati Bengals (5-2)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

The Bengals could easily make a move at the deadline, and nobody will bat an eye, but on the surface, there’s no one spot on the depth chart that stands out as a “must-add”. That said, don’t be surprised if they ship out last year’s first-round pick Shemar Stewart. He was a healthy scratch, and things have not gone well for him since arriving in Cincinnati. If they do add, another edge rusher could make sense. 

12. Los Angeles Rams (4-4)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers (Responsibly)

General manager Les Snead has long been a proponent of “F them picks”, but every GM has their limits, and the Rams would be wise to play it safe this deadline. Despite a slow start, they have a favorable upcoming schedule, and most of their key injuries should be back over the next month. That said, a value addition at either receiver or defensive tackle could make some sense. 

13. New England Patriots (5-3)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

Considering their injuries on the interior, could the Patriots take a swing for a rental offensive lineman? Even without Romeo Doubs, their pass-catchers feel “good enough”. Defensively, they are in a good spot, but another body on the defensive line is always a need for Super Bowl-caliber teams. Overall, the Patriots are in a good spot if they can get healthy, but the interior offensive line feels like a spot where they could make a move, even if it’s just a rental. 

14. Seattle Seahawks (4-4)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat (Following the addition of Quenton Nelson)

In theory, the Seahawks have plenty of compensatory picks coming their way after losing multiple players to free agency. Still, they just dealt a third- and future fifth-round pick away to land Nelson. More than likely, they’ll settle with what they have, but if they do make a move, some additional tackle depth or another tight end could make sense. 

15. New York Giants (4-2-1)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

All things considered, the Giants have had a great year. Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart went down in Week 2, and despite a 2-0 start, it felt like it was just a matter of time before the bottom fell out. Instead, they’ve maintained their pace in the NFC East and have a legitimate shot to win the division. With that in mind, this is not the year to trade away valuable picks. Even if they can win the division, the chances of doing much in a loaded NFC are not great. Make this season a strong building block for 2027. 

16. Cleveland Browns (5-3)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

In theory, the Browns could make a move or two, especially since they are far better than expected. That said, even if they make the playoffs, the chances of them making some noise are slim to none. Ultimately, they should stay the course and build this team through the draft or trades for players they control longer than half a season. Cleveland has been a great story, but there’s no need to start going all-in quite yet. 

17. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

Things have been tough following a 3-0 start to open the season. Even so, there’s plenty to like about where the Raiders are headed, and we haven’t even seen No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza get his first NFL start yet. Barring a hard course-correction, the Raiders are unlikely to challenge for a playoff spot, but that’s OK. Most teams with rookie quarterbacks drafted this high rarely do. They could look to unload a piece or two; heck, maybe a good offensive lineman comes available that makes sense. Outside of that, they are probably better off standing pat and seeing how the rest of the season plays out. 

18. Dallas Cowboys (3-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers (Even If They Shouldn’t Be)

Owner Jerry Jones has proven to be more reckless the older he gets, and why should this deadline be any different? At some point, you have to trust that the offense will stabilize, but the defense is still in need of more help. An edge rusher would make the most sense, but even some defensive tackle depth could add some value. The NFC East is still winnable, but the Cowboys should tread carefully over the next week. 

19. Baltimore Ravens (4-4)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

As long as quarterback Lamar Jackson is healthy, the Ravens will be playoff contenders. The issue is that Jackson has been healthy, and now, with his thumb injury and a .500 record, this season feels all but lost. Baltimore could sell off some veteran pieces if they want to, or they could wait until the offseason before making any rash decisions. Either way, the outlook of their season changed drastically with Lamar’s thumb injury. 

20. Carolina Panthers (3-4)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers 

Injuries are catching up to the Panthers, and without an offense scoring 30 points per game, they’ll struggle to win games. That said, an improved secondary should help leave a little more margin for error. The trick here is that they must be confident quarterback Bryce Young can get back on track, along with the offense. If so, making a move for a rental cornerback would make plenty of sense. 

21. Houston Texans (2-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Could Go Either Way

In theory, the Texans should be pushing for a playoff spot, but following a slow start, it’s worth wondering how much of their future they should mortgage for a chance to get back to the playoffs. Because of how their roster is constructed, adding makes more sense than subtracting, but even then, what’s the overall upside for this season? After the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade, this feels like a deadline they should sit out. 

22. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Stand Pat

Winners of two in a row, the Bucs are somehow right back in the divisional race, despite quarterback Baker Mayfield not completing a pass on Sunday. That said, this team isn’t destined for much success, even if they win a bad NFC South. At this point, they should probably sell, but after two straight wins, standing pat and watching it play out seems like the kind of approach a team on thin ice would take. They’d have some pieces to sell if they choose to, but I have a feeling they’ll stick with what they have and see how it goes. 

23. Atlanta Falcons (3-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Buyers

With the Panthers’ recent struggles, the Falcons are right back in the divisional race, and I might even argue that they should be the favorites heading into Week 8. That, of course, is assuming that quarterback Michael Penix can stay healthy. Adding a more effective WR2 should be a top priority, even if it’s a rental. Atlanta is better than expected, and they can make a move or two without breaking the bank. 

24. New Orleans Saints (2-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Could Go Either Way

Even with a similar record to the Buccaneers, the Saints find themselves in a different position. On the surface, this team doesn’t look good enough to buy, but it is a young group with upside that a team like Tampa Bay doesn’t. Continued development at quarterback is key, but if they can make an affordable move or two for longer-term pieces, it might be worth it. After all, general manager Mickey Loomis isn’t known for being conservative, even when he should be. 

25. Arizona Cardinals (3-5)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

Similar to Miami, the Cardinals are in a spot where they are at the start of their rebuild, but don’t have many valuable pieces to sell off. Landing a second-round pick for Marvin Harrison Jr. was a great move, but additional picks would be ideal. Veteran running back Tyler Allgeier should draw some interest, but dealing veteran defensive linemen makes the most sense, and they have plenty to offer. Josh Sweat is the marquee name, but both Roy Lopez and Andrew Billings could make sense for late-round picks too. A few other names could shake out, but again, Arizona doesn’t have a ton to offer without trading away from their core. 

26. Washington Commanders (2-4-1)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

Technically, the Commanders still aren’t out of it in the NFC East. Even so, the chances of them figuring things out and making enough of a run to push for a playoff spot feel highly unlikely. The Commanders will have plenty of tough decisions to make in the offseason, but unloading some veteran names for mid-to-late-round draft capital feels like the play. Stefon Diggs and Daron Payne felt like their best pieces, but Payne’s season-ending injury kills one of those targets. Instead, don’t rule out moving other defensive veterans like Tim Settle or even Rasul Douglas. 

27. New York Jets (2-6)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

The Jets are a better team than last year, but their loss to the Dolphins in Week 7 shows how far they have to go. Although nobody should expect them to sell off to the level that they did last season, offloading some veteran pieces could make sense, even if it’s for future draft capital in 2028 or beyond. A reunion with Nahshon Wright and Chicago could make sense, and it’s worth wondering if they’ll take other players like Kingsley Enagbare, Minkah Fitzpatrick, or maybe even T’Vondre Sweat for the right price. They already have plenty of draft capital, but why not add more if it makes sense? 

28. Philadelphia Eagles (2-6)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

Nobody knows what the future holds for the Eagles, but at this point, 2026 is a lost cause. Quarterback Tanner McKey isn’t going to win many ballgames, and the Eagles have a few rentals that could earn them additional draft capital for next season. I’d keep an eye on players like Riq Woolen, Landon Dickerson, and Dallas Goedert. Maybe even upside players like Moro Ojomo and a surprise like Saquon Barkley (if he’s healthy). General manager Howie Roseman has never been shy about making bold decisions. 

29. Indianapolis Colts (2-6)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

The Colts kicked off a crazy week by trading both Nelson and Buckner in the matter of hours. Both players were cornerstone pieces, and although neither brought back hefty returns, it’s a sign that they are tearing this roster down to the studs. Interim general manager Ed Dodds shouldn’t stop there, especially with players like Josh Downs and Grover Stewart among others who are set to hit free agency in March. Jonathan Taylor is another player who could be dealt in the next week. Like the Jets last year, the Colts have picked a direction and should keep committing to it.  

30. Tennessee Titans (1-7)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

There’s no other way to put this: through eight games, 2026 has been a complete disaster for the Titans. Cam Ward has not developed as planned, and despite being big players in free agency, this first-year coaching staff isn’t getting enough out of this roster. Following the trade of Simmons for a pair of first-round picks, offloading more veteran pieces, especially on defense, feels almost necessary. Jermaine Johnson, Solomon Thomas, and Alontae Taylor are all defenders to keep an eye on, and maybe even Calvin Ridley on the offensive side of the ball. The teardown shouldn’t stop at Simmons. 

31. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers

Reports out of Los Angeles have been less than ideal, especially after such a poor start. Although the word is that they aren’t ready to offload aging veterans or valuable pieces, I find that almost impossible to believe. At worst, moving on from players like Khalil Mack, Dalvin Tomlinson, and maybe even Donte Jackson makes too much sense not to do. The one “surprise” name that could move for the right price is edge rusher Tuli Tuipulotu. 

32. Miami Dolphins (1-6)

Deadline Status (and needs): Sellers 

When a team is in the early stages of an extensive rebuild, selling off additional pieces makes the most sense. Miami lacks talent in most areas, but they have a few defenders that could be on the move for the right price. Zach Sieler and Josh Uche make the most sense as aging veterans, but Chop Robinson could be traded too for the right price. We’ll see what the Dolphins do, but a move or two for additional draft capital makes plenty of sense.

item.title: The Hot Read: Mike McCarthy is having the last laugh
item.description: The Pittsburgh Steelers and Mike McCarthy are proving everyone wrong.
item.content:encoded:
A funny thing happened on the way to the Pittsburgh Steelers’ funeral that all your favorite talking heads planned during the offseason – Mike McCarthy kept winning. Because all Mike McCarthy has done in his career as a head coach is win.

He did it for 13 years as the head coach of the Green Bay Packers, where he became the second-winningest head coach in franchise history, his 135 wins trailing only Curly Lambeau. In those 13 years, the Packers went to the playoffs nine times and won the Super Bowl in 2010.

After his time in Green Bay came to an end, he took a gap year in 2019 before landing with the Dallas Cowboys in 2020. In five seasons with Dallas, he led the Cowboys to the playoffs three times, including three consecutive 12-win seasons from 2021-23. Despite that success, the Cowboys allowed his contract to expire and didn’t bring him back – how’s Brian Schottenheimer doing, by the way? Once again, he took a gap year and sat out the 2025 season. And while McCarthy was taking a pit stop away from football, the Pittsburgh Steelers were failing to catch the leaders of the race.

The Steelers were never bad under Mike Tomlin. In case you haven’t heard, he never had a losing season in his 19 years as head coach. However, the Steelers haven’t won a playoff game since the 2016 season. And despite Tomlin’s consistency and ability to back his way into a playoff berth, the lack of playoff success, as well as an inability to field a high-caliber offense, kept the Steelers in a stage of elite mediocrity.

And even so, the vast majority of national voices often scoffed at the idea of Pittsburgh moving on from Tomlin. “He would get another job in five minutes,” they would all cry out in unison as if Tomlin and the Steelers kept banging their head against a wall expecting different results.

But after yet another blowout playoff defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in the 2026 wild card round, Tomlin stepped down as head coach. History told us that Pittsburgh would go the younger route to replace the former longest-tenured head coach in major American sports. Chuck Noll was 37 when he was hired by the Steelers in 1969. Bill Cowher was 34 when he was hired back in 1992, as was Tomlin when he was hired in 2007. Several names like Jesse Minter, Anthony Weaver, Chris Shula, and Nate Scheelhaase were all circled as the potential next coach of the Steelers, but it was the 62 year-old McCarthy who got the job to the ire of many. Almost instantly, those same talking heads who refused to ever criticize Mike Tomlin ridiculed the McCarthy hire, metaphorically nudging one another with their elbows and trying to contain their laughter.

“Hard to imagine a more uninspired choice for a franchise in the Steelers’ exact position.,” Robert Mays of The Athletic said.

ESPN’s Dan Orlovsky went as far to say that the Steelers pairing McCarthy with Aaron Rodgers would be “the worst decision Pittsburgh could make.”

Unfortunately, most walks of life adapt the rules of high school. There are the cool kids, and the ones who are deemed to be uncool. National media as a consensus decided long ago that Mike McCarthy wasn’t allowed to sit at their table, but contemporaries who first became head coaches in the same era as him – like Tomlin and Sean Payton – get treated as if they invented the forward pass despite McCarthy having more playoff wins than both of them and a Super Bowl ring.

So what has “the worst decision Pittsburgh could make” done through the first half of the season? Well, the Steelers are 6-2 and sit atop the AFC North at their bye week. Their six wins are tied for the most in the AFC, and they sit just a half game back of the No. 1 seed in the AFC. In the midst of their four game win streak, their offense ranks first in EPA per rush since Week 5, second in rushing yards, and third in yards per carry. Overall, Pittsburgh’s offense ranks seventh in EPA per play over that span and ninth in success rate while averaging just under 26 points per game. In conjunction with the offense coming to life has been the emergence of Jaylen Warren as a superstar. The former undrafted product out of Oklahoma State is third in the NFL in scrimmage yards behind only Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and he leads all running backs in total EPA.

Not only is the offense thriving, but so, too is the defense. A year after finishing 26th in total defense, the Steelers are sixth in the league in total defense through eight games. They are also tied for fifth in defensive EPA per play and lead the NFL with 26 sacks, with T.J. Watt leading the league with 7.5 sacks.

Everyone placed Pittsburgh in the metaphorical guillotine when they hired McCarthy. Meanwhile, his aforementioned fellow long-time head coach Sean Payton is currently fielding an offense that currently ranks 30th in yards per game while still receiving universal praise and having zero fault placed upon his shoulders. Despite all the outside criticism, all McCarthy and the Steelers have done is win. Everyone swore they would collapse when the Tomlin era ended, but they’ve gotten better instead, and McCarthy is getting the last laugh.

That was the cold open – this is the Hot Read.

Three and out

The Bears are the team to beat in the NFC

In a conference that is lacking in truly elite teams, the Chicago Bears have claimed the right to be called the top team in the NFC after their blowout win over the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night.

Entering Week 8, no quarterback had topped 200 yards passing on Seattle’s defense. Caleb Williams went 24-of-34 for 247 yards and a touchdown, while the Bears’ run game added 126 yards on the ground. The bigger story, though, with the Bears isn’t their offense, which everyone expected to be great, it’s their defense of which no one expected to be great.

Entering the season, Aaron Schatz’ FTN Football Almanac projected the Bears to have the worst defense in football. And this is no shot whatsoever at Aaron, it’s a credit to defensive coordinator Dennis Allen for the job he’s done with a unit that lacked any big names entering the season. After eight weeks, the Bears are sixth in defensive EPA per play and third in defensive success rate. Most importantly, though, the Bears are the league’s best defense on third down, sporting the best defensive EPA per play in the NFL. Their defensive success rate on third down is also four percent higher than the second-place Vikings. Oh yeah, and they just traded for Jeffery Simmons.

With how dynamic Chicago’s offense is, balanced out by a truly great defense, it’s easy to put them atop the NFC hierarchy when the rest of the conference is largely swapping places by the week.

The AFC remains wide open

While the NFC is pretty cut-and-dry on who its top contenders currently are, the AFC remains wide open, as no team has looked truly dominant through eight weeks. The Buffalo Bills currently hold the No. 1 seed with a 6-1 record, but they have yet to look truly complete. Their offensive play-calling got very messy against a Ravens team that was down to its third quarterback until finally pulling away in the fourth quarter. Additionally, their defense is putrid, ranking 26th in EPA per play. The Broncos are the leaders of the AFC West, but their offense is as intimidating as a barn full of newborn kittens. Pittsburgh’s run game is elite, and they field one of the league’s top defenses, but there is something missing in the passing game that leaves you wanting more. The Bengals just made the Titans offense look like the ‘99 Rams. The Chiefs are throwing to hot dog vendors and Andy Reid is simply being outcoached.

The most complete team in the conference is the Jaguars. They just dropped 42 points on the Colts, which marks the third time they’ve scored at least 34 points in a game this season, and their defense ranks third in EPA per play. However, Jacksonville hasn’t won a playoff game since the 2021 season, and not being one of the blue blood teams in the conference over the last decade is leading to them being overshadowed.

Overall, the AFC has eight teams with 5+ wins compared to just five such teams in the NFC. The conference remains wide open as we begin the trudge through the winter months.

The Ravens should think about life after Lamar Jackson

It’s never going to be popular to suggest that a team should trade a two-time MVP, but there is certainly a case to be made for the Ravens to do just that.

Lamar Jackson is on IR with a thumb injury that could end his season. This comes after he missed three games with an ankle injury, which led the Ravens to go 1-2 during his absence. This marks the fourth time in six seasons in which Jackson will miss extended time. He missed five games in both the 2021 and 2022 seasons, and missed four games in 2025, With his ankle injury and IR designation, he will miss seven games at the bare minimum in 2026, with it being very likely that the number will be much higher.

Jackson will be a free agent in 2028 if the Ravens don’t give him an extension. This season was largely seen as a prove-it type of year for the former first-round pick to show that he could stay healthy and be relied on to lead the Ravens for the extended future. But unfortunately for Lamar, the writing on the wall is becoming clearer. If he is indeed done for the season, he’ll be 30 the next time he touches a football field. 30 years old with just a single AFC Championship Game appearance and no Super Bowl berths. Are the Ravens really going to be itching to extend a 30 year-old oft-injured mobile quarterback to a $60+ million per year deal? Probably not, nor should they.

If Baltimore wanted to move on from Jackson, they can certainly do so next year. Per Over The Cap, trading him would save the Ravens just under $10 million against the cap. A restructure of Nnamdi Madubuike’s contract could save them $14 million against the cap, and letting go of a declining Roquan Smith would save them $20 million. Add in a release of Marlon Humphrey with a post June-1 designation, and the Ravens would be cap compliant, and that’s before a whole other slew of other adjustments they could make to free up even more money, i.e. Trey Hendrickson and Kyle Hamilton to create roughly $17 million in cap space.

Plus, a trade of Jackson would kick a rebuild into high gear. He would still garner two first-round picks, which would give Baltimore a lot of high-end ammunition to re-tool for the future. Considering it’s looking like they could be drafting in the top 10 in 2027, an additional pair of firsts over the next two years would give them more assets to find their eventual new franchise quarterback.

None of this is to say that Jackson is all of a sudden a bad football player, but sometimes it’s just time. The Harbaugh-Jackson era came to an end without a Super Bowl appearance, and Jackson is all but certainly past the peak of his career. On a new team that has money to spend for high-end weapons to put around Jackson, that team could contend. The Ravens, though, don’t have the financial ability to do that. With a new coaching staff currently fielding a roster largely full of aging players, ripping the band-aid and starting fresh is the right move.

One play that changed everything

The Chiefs looked poised to put at least three points on the board late in the fourth quarter. With 2:40 remaining in the fourth quarter, Kansas City had the ball at the Broncos’ 29 yard-line on 3rd-and-2. While unable to find an open receiver, Patrick Mahomes ran to his right and inexplicably took a sack from Alex Singleton instead of throwing the ball away. The sack took what would have been a 46-yard field goal and made it a 54-yard field goal for Harrison Butler, which he missed. The Broncos took over and scored a go-ahead touchdown, going up by four. Had Mahomes not taken the sack, perhaps Butker makes the field goal and Kansas City is able to kick a game-winner at the gun instead of having to go for a touchdown.

Buy or sell

Buy: The Bengals should trade for Jonathan Taylor

Cincinnati has zero semblance of a run game. A good bit of that is definitely due to their refusal to ever go under center, but a back like Taylor, who can beat teams up as a runner or receiver, would make them an even bigger offensive juggernaut than they already are.

Sell: The Cleveland Browns

The real Browns stood up on Sunday. Jared Verse talked all week just to finish with more suplexes received than tackles. Through eight games, Steelers undrafted defensive lineman Kevin Jobity has more sacks than Verse, who has yet to register one all season. The offense also failed to reach the end zone as Deshaun Watson was sacked eight times and looked much more like the quarterback we’ve grown to know.

Buy: The Cowboys should fire Christian Parker

I’ve seen enough. Over the last 15 months, the Cowboys have traded for/drafted the likes of Kenny Clark, Rashan Gary, Quinnen Williams, Caleb Downs, and Joey Porter Jr. Despite all those moves, though they are the league’s worst defense, ranking dead last in EPA per play and giving up the most rushing yards in the NFL. It’s clear that first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker is in over his head. Move on from him, give the interim job to Mike Pettine, and see if he can salvage the second half of the season.

Sell: The Minnesota Vikings

We led last week’s Hot Read with the Vikings and how they were a paper tiger, and that is still very much the case. They failed to score 20 points against a Lions defense that ranks 31st in EPA per play, and it marks the fourth time they’ve failed to reach the 20-point threshold this season. Kyler Murray is dealing with a hamstring injury, and honestly? The Vikings should bench him even if he is healthy enough to play. This offense had far more juice when Carson Wentz was running the show. Of the 35 quarterbacks who have played 100 snaps, Murray ranks 26th in EPA per play and 28th in pass success rate.

Prediction to track

NFL predictions to track

  • Steelers will trade Joey Porter Jr: Correct
  • Rams will beat Broncos handedly: Incorrect
  • Lions will blowout Panthers: Incorrect
  • Marvin Harrison Jr and Brian Thomas Jr will be traded: Half correct
  • Jordan Love will have explosive game as Packers defeat Cowboys: Correct
  • Fan will rush the field in Steelers vs. Saints with political message: Incorrect
  • Jaguars will beat Cols by two scores (and Shane Steichen will be fired): Correct (incorrect)

Well, we finally hit on a blowout prediction, so we can consider that curse lifted. Picking the Jaguars to have consecutive blowouts would be too easy, as they are projected to face you, the reader, at quarterback on Thursday when they host the Ravens. So instead, let’s be bold and make one that probably won’t happen, but is fun to fantasy book.

The Jets travel to Kansas City in Week 9. After losing to the Chiefs, Garrett Wilson stays put because the Jets trade him to Kansas City in exchange for a first-round pick. God knows the Chiefs need pass-catchers, as Xavier Worthy somehow finds himself in another state at least once a game, and the less said about Andrew Armstrong and Jalen Royals, the better. The Chiefs take a swing and get a legitimate No. 1 for Patrick Mahomes as they chase Super Bowl No. 4.

item.title: Fantasy Football Panic Meter: Ravens are in trouble going into Week 9 after latest Lamar Jackson injury
item.description: Ray Garvin is worried about the Ravens, Vikings, but cautions not to give up on the Jaguars WR in his latest Panic Meter.
item.content:encoded:
It's getting harder to give some of these offenses the benefit of the doubt. Coming out of Week 8, I'm sorting through where I'm willing to stay patient and where I'd rather make a move before things get worse.

Baltimore Ravens offense: Coping Corner

We're in the early stages of Coping Corner with the Baltimore Ravens offense. Lamar Jackson injured his thumb on Baltimore's first offensive play in Week 8 and is now headed to injured reserve. That alone would have been a deflating afternoon for the Ravens and fantasy managers counting on this offense. Then Tyler Huntley went down, leaving undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano to finish the game. Everybody loves the backup until the backup becomes the starter. We're now at the backup's backup.

This went from zero to 100 real quick.

You're still playing Derrick Henry, but I'm lowering my expectations. His 53 rushing yards and a touchdown gave you something usable, though that score came after a turnover put Baltimore at Buffalo's 17-yard line. Without Lamar, sustaining drives and creating those scoring opportunities becomes a much bigger concern. Henry can still give you a productive afternoon, but it doesn't feel like you have that same high-upside running back anymore.

The passing game? Man, it doesn't feel good. Zay Flowers ran 30 routes and earned five targets without catching a pass. Mark Andrews caught three passes for 14 yards, and to me, he looks well past his prime. I wasn't feeling good about him before Lamar went down. Losing Jackson only makes it harder to see where the production is going to come from. Any breakout thoughts you had about Ja'Kobi Lane took a hit, too. He ran 21 routes and saw one target.

Baltimore finished with 144 total yards. Fagnano completed 10-of-21 passes for 91 yards and an interception. This is the environment we're asking our fantasy players to produce in right now.

Yes, you're probably still playing Flowers. I'm not telling you to bench him regardless of your alternatives. But I would absolutely be open to trading him if someone is still valuing him like he's catching passes from a healthy Lamar. I want a usable starter back, but I'm willing to have that conversation before we get another look at how difficult this passing game could become. Losing Lamar takes the life out of this offense, and it's hard to see how things get much better anytime soon. With Andrews and Lane, I'm looking at my alternatives.

Minnesota Vikings offense: Some Panic

There was enough from Kyler Murray to keep Minnesota out of Total Panic. There wasn't enough to make me feel great about the entire offense.

Murray threw for 210 yards and two touchdowns while adding 35 yards on the ground. T.J. Hockenson caught four of his five targets for 58 yards and a touchdown, continuing to give us reasons to trust this connection. Through seven games, Hockenson has a 20.4% target share and is averaging 2.03 yards per route run. I'm comfortable treating him as a weekly top-12 tight end.

Justin Jefferson scored, but five catches for 33 yards isn't what you drafted him for. His frustration showed on the sideline, and he declined to speak with reporters afterward. He had nine targets and a 32.1% target share, so the ball was going his way. It still wasn't turning into the kind of production you expect from Jefferson. I understand the frustration, and I'm sure his fantasy managers do, too.

The secondary pieces are where my confidence starts to drop. Jordan Addison's season has been disappointing, although this game deserves some credit: eight targets, three catches and 66 yards while matching Jefferson's 33 routes. I'm not going to call that a disappearing act. I do need more consistency before I feel good counting on him.

The running game gave us much less to work with. Jordan Mason carried eight times for 20 yards. Aaron Jones Sr. managed 22 yards on five attempts. That's 42 rushing yards between them, with Murray individually outrushing either back.

Hockenson and Jefferson stay in your lineup. Beyond those two, I have questions about how much dependable fantasy production this offense can support.

Carolina Panthers offense: Some Panic

We're a couple of weeks removed from Tetairoa McMillan's monster day, and now we're back to wondering when Carolina will put the whole thing together.

McMillan finished with six catches for 58 yards against Green Bay. The frustrating part is that the workload was there. He had 11 targets, a 31.4% target share and more than half of Carolina's targeted air yards. That is plenty of opportunity to deliver a much bigger afternoon.

Bryce Young completed 23-of-41 passes for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. He was sacked six times. Carolina was also without offensive linemen Damien Lewis and Torricelli Simpkins III, which certainly didn't help an offense already struggling to turn opportunities into production.

I've got Some Panic with McMillan, but those 11 targets keep me from recommending a massive change. His season target share sits at 26.4%. He's still getting the kind of involvement I want to bet on, even if living with the results has been frustrating.

Jalen Coker belongs in Some Panic, too. His touchdown helped, but it accounted for 26 of his 36 receiving yards. He caught two passes on five targets. I'm glad we got the score. I'm not suddenly comfortable with the weekly floor.

Chuba Hubbard gets No Panic from me. He handled 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown, then added seven receptions for 38 yards. That's 29 touches and 119 scrimmage yards in a game where the passing offense struggled. He kept finding ways to produce.

I'm still playing McMillan and Hubbard. With Coker, I'm accepting a much wider range of outcomes. You're going to have to live with some volatility here rather than overhaul your lineup.

Parker Washington: No Panic

I'm not panicking on P-Wash. I am going to keep reminding people that Jacksonville doesn't feel like an offense with the same clear-cut No. 1 option every week. I talked about this with Matt Harmon on the Data Dump Tuesday show. When everything is clicking for Washington, the usage can be outstanding. But Lawrence will get the ball to the open man, and that isn't going to be Washington every week.

Against Indianapolis, he caught one pass for 16 yards on two targets and added 10 rushing yards. Jacksonville won 42-7 after leading 28-0 at halftime. Trevor Lawrence attempted just 14 passes before his day was over early in the fourth quarter. Bhayshul Tuten ran for 104 yards and scored both on the ground and through the air. This offense had plenty working without needing a big Washington game.

In his last game before the bye, Washington caught four passes for 64 yards against Houston but still drew 11 targets. The fantasy results weren't what you wanted in either game, but the opportunities were very different.

Across seven games, Washington has a 24.5% target share and has drawn a target on 25.3% of his routes. We also saw him turn six catches into 124 yards and two touchdowns against Philadelphia. That's the ceiling I'm still betting on.

To me, Washington still has the highest receiving ceiling in this offense. I'm embracing the variance that comes with it. One bad afternoon in a blowout versus a terrible Colts team isn't enough to move me off him.

item.title: Most common players on eliminated teams from Week 8 in Yahoo Fantasy Death leagues — plus FAB waiver wire advice
item.description: Death Leagues have claimed more star players. Fantasy football analyst Scott Pianowski advises you on how to approach the waiver wire in Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
Every week I'll examine the most common NFL players on the teams eliminated in Yahoo Death Leagues, trying to figure out where the puck is headed. I will also offer some FAB advice ($1,000 cap is the Yahoo default), but please remember this area is highly context-sensitive and manager-specific.

Waiver strategy in Death Leagues

For the first six weeks, I used this space to talk up the long game. I like to trust myself (and my depth) in the early weeks, and take heart that it's not that difficult to beat just one team when the league is still large.

The rules are starting to shift now. Eight of your opponents are checked out for the year. Keep in mind the bye weeks are here — the Steelers and Titans don't play in Week 9. Injuries also continue to mount , part of why these games are so challenging, and downright cruel at times.

In the first month of Death League season, I'm going to trust the size of the league and be confident I can beat just one of the teams. As such, I'm not proactive on early offers. I'm definitely more proactive now, but remember that the strength of each cut team becomes much stronger as we get deep into the season. Be very careful not to to cripple your remaining budget for the future.

Understanding FAB recommendations

I'll still offer bidding in three buckets, and you'll need to season the recommendations to taste. You know your context and league habits better than an outsider would. But just know the immediacy has stepped up a bit. I still think it's a mistake to spend all of your money in the present — the wire gets stronger and stronger in every passing week — but I also understand the gravity at hand. So don't be afraid to get in there with some competitive offers.

My weekly FAB recommendations will come in three buckets:

Proactive: This means you highly covet this player, perhaps might even need this player. I realize these offers might not win if someone in your league is lighting money on fire, but as described above, that's often a short-sighted mistake in this format.

Reactive: This means you desire the player but the offer has to make sense for your short- or long-term strategy.

Keep Them Honest: This is an offer that is not designed to win, but might surprisingly land a player if your opponents are distracted by other talent available or unexpectedly passive that week. I often compare notes with other experienced Death League players and we're surprised at how often the Keep Them Honest offers actually win (this is also a portable strategy for regular season-long leagues; you never know when strange market behavior will come about).

One last note: Understand that the FAB recommendations are with the assumption that you won't be making offers for every available player.

Week 8's top-10 players on eliminated teams

1. WR Zay Flowers, Ravens (24.3%)

He’s been unstoppable most of the year, but the latest Lamar Jackson injury sunk him in Buffalo. Tyler Huntley also might miss multiple weeks, which means the Ravens offense could be under water. But Flowers is such a talent, we have to keep the light on for him.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $125 proactive

  • $60 reactive

  • $20 keep them honest

2. RB Jonathan Taylor, Colts (22.2%)

He played on about 60% of the snaps in the blowout loss to Jacksonville. Taylor’s value is likely to rebound for one of two reasons; either he’ll be dealt to a contender, or he’ll stay with the Colts and thrive on a favorable second-half schedule. But the next week or so could be bumpy as everything sorts out.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $235 proactive

  • $130 reactive

  • $70 keep them honest

3. QB Lamar Jackson, Ravens (21.8%)

A busted thumb has Jackson on IR and it’s possible he’s done for the year. Baltimore’s season could be on life support, too.

FAB Recommendation:

  • No bid

4. WR Drake London, Falcons (20.7%)

Between Tampa raindrops and a nightmare day for Michael Penix Jr. (four interceptions), the Atlanta passing game never got off the ground in Week 8. The Bengals present a good rebound spot this week, but then it’s a mess: Chiefs, bye week, Vikings. London’s rep remains the same; he’s a very good player, but just short of a superstar.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $150 proactive

  • $80 reactive

  • $30 keep them honest

5. RB Bijan Robinson, Falcons (19.1%)

His touchdown slump has reached four games, and he’s failed to make double-digit fantasy points in two of three starts. It’s hard to fault Robinson much when he’s still averaging 5.2 YPC, but the Falcons need to find more ways to get him involved as a receiver.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $300 proactive

  • $165 reactive

  • $100 keep them honest

6. RB Javonte Willams, Cowboys (17.2%)

The volume was lovely against the Cardinals, but Williams struggled to find running lanes or goal-line success. The upcoming schedule is favorable, starting with a date at Indy in Week 9. Williams remains a solid cornerstone for any format.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $180 proactive

  • $90 reactive

  • $40 keep them honest

7. WR Parker Washington, Jaguars (16.7%)

His target share has been erratic most of the year, but sometimes you have to bet on talent. The upcoming schedule is favorable (Baltimore, a couple of Tennessee games) and at least Washington is tied to a star QB and a shrewd play-caller.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $165 proactive

  • $70 reactive

  • $25 keep them honest

8. RB Christian McCaffrey, 49ers (16.1%)

Hard to fault a guy on his bye week. McCaffrey’s efficiency is no longer dreamy, but he’s a bell cow on a scoring offense, so cut the big check.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $280 proactive

  • $150 reactive

  • $100 keep them honest

9. WR George Pickens, Cowboys (15.5%)

Perhaps hamstring and shoulder injuries kept Pickens down in the shocking loss to Arizona. Owner Jerry Jones is calling for Pickens to get more work forward, an interesting spin on the “squeaky wheel” narrative. The Cowboys still have a narrow target tree, so Pickens makes sense as a proactive get.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $170 proactive

  • $75 reactive

  • $30 keep them honest

10. QB Brock Purdy, 49ers (15.2%)

Given how injured the Niners are at receiver, the Week 8 bye wasn’t unwelcome. If Mike Evans can stay on the field, Purdy can still be an elite fantasy option. But if Evans has any hiccups, all bets are off.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $120 proactive

  • $45 reactive

  • $8-10 keep them honest

item.title: Numbers Never Lie: 5 Chiefs stats to know from loss to Broncos
item.description: What are the most important statistics from Kansas City’s recent losses?
item.content:encoded:
Numbers never lie, right?

There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect from the Kansas City Chiefs moving forward.

1. No Chiefs defender earned more than one QB pressure in Denver

Five Chiefs players tied for the team lead in quarterback pressures against the Denver Broncos, according to PFF. All with just one.

  • Defensive end R Mason Thomas
  • Defensive end Ashton Gillotte
  • Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah
  • Defensive end George Karlaftis
  • Nose tackle Khyiris Tonga

Karlaftis recorded one sack, but PFF’s metrics show no other hits on quarterback Bo Nix.

The biggest absence on the list is defensive tackle Chris Jones, who has generated pressure at one of the lowest rates among Chiefs defenders this season. In the two losses, Jones recorded just one pressure and no tackles; PFF marked him with two missed tackles against the Seahawks.

2. Chiefs wideouts average 5 yards per target against Broncos

On 17 passes thrown their way and 13 completions, Chiefs wideouts averaged just 5.2 yards per target against the Broncos, even with No. 1 receiver Rashee Rice (7 catches for 53 yards) back in the lineup. Over the last two weeks, Chiefs wideouts have averaged just 4.5 yards per pass.

In the Week 1 beatdown of the Broncos, Chiefs wideouts gained just 37 yards on 10 targets.

As defenses have seen more tape on Kansas City’s offense this season, the receivers have become more necessary to maintain a rhythm and finish drives. Many of the unit’s shortcomings recently have fallen on the lack of consistency from the receiver position; specifically, Xavier Worthy. He has not stepped up in the way the team needed after losing the primary deep threat in the scheme, Tyquan Thornton.

3. Nohl Williams and Kristian Fulton allowed just 29 receiving yards in Denver

Over six passes thrown at Chiefs’ starting cornerbacks Nohl Williams and Kristian Fulton, filling in for the injured Mansoor Delane (shoulder), they caught only three passes for 29 yards (only 9 yards gained after the catch).

Fulton was called for defensive pass interference early on, but overall, the Chiefs shut down the perimeter against wide receivers Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle. Denver found success through the air only by targeting the middle of the field, where safety Chamarri Conner and linebacker Nick Bolton allowed big-time catches in crucial spots.

4. Chiefs tie season-high mark with 28 under-center plays against Broncos

A week after running just 12 plays from under center, a season-low mark, the Chiefs’ offense re-established its identity in Denver and tied the season-high number of 28 plays run from under center; the team matched it against the Miami Dolphins in Week 3.

Patrick Mahomes also attempted the most passes from under center in any game this season, dropping back 14 times.

However, Kansas City averaged just 4.5 yards per play from under center, the second-lowest rate of the year behind the poor showing in Seattle.

It may not have been the most efficient game, but the offense looked much better than it did in Seattle, and getting back to what worked through the first five games of the year felt like a big factor in that.

5. Kenneth Walker has 105 rushing yards combined in two losses

Over 35 rushing attempts against the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos, lead back Kenneth Walker has averaged just three yards per carry, gained six first downs and only found room for one 10-yard run

In the previous five games, Walker averaged 5.8 yards per carry, moved the chains 37 times and had 20 runs of 10 or more yards.

Seattle and Denver certainly found a blueprint for limiting Walker on the ground, and the Chiefs looked better from week to week at countering that attention with an effective passing game. In Denver, there were good play designs to get the ball in the hands of running backs or tight ends off play-action or misdirection that didn’t show up against the Seahawks.

However, is the emergence of running back Emmett Johnson as a pass-catching playmaker enough to overcome the next elite defense that shuts Walker down completely? That’s where the logic in a trade-deadline move comes from.

item.title: NFL Week 9 power rankings: Lions’ rise continues but still have doubters
item.description: A look at where the Detroit Lions sit in the the NFL’s 2026 Week 9 power rankings.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions (5-2) have now won three in a row and beaten NFC North rivals—the Green Bay Packers in Week 7 and the Minnesota Vikings in Week 8—in back-to-back games.

The Lions’ balanced roster and adaptable coaching staff allow them to stay competitive with any opponent, and as we have seen in each of the three previous wins, they can beat an opponent in a variety of ways. Against the Cardinals, the Lions unleashed their passing attack; against the Packers, they controlled possessions and the clock; and last Sunday, they matched the Vikings’ aggression with an attacking run game and dominated on the ground. With each win, the Lions’ defense has steadily improved, though many national analysts are still looking at season-long stats instead of what they’ve done recently.

In this week’s power rankings, the Lions moved up in every ranking; however, they’re still one holdout away from being a consensus top-10 team. Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings.

Sports Illustrated: 4 (Previous rank: 7)

From Connor Orr:

Drew Petzing has been on my ascending head coaches list but has put himself on many others after a sterling performance against the Vikings. Petzing managed to get the job done against Brian Flores and add a flourish, a particular feat that seems almost impossible given how talented this Minnesota defense is.

NFL.com: 5 (Previous rank: 11)

From Nick Shook:

This might not age well, given the serious injury questions facing the Lions, but I’m giving them the boost because of how they finished their victory over the previously undefeated Vikings. Facing a 15-12 deficit in the fourth quarter, Detroit sliced right through Minnesota’s terrifying defense with apparent ease, leaning on Jahmyr Gibbs before finishing the drive with a beautiful touchdown pass from Jared Goff to Jameson Williams. The Lions won by sticking to their offensive identity, getting another encouraging showing from the defense and outlasting the Vikings in a victory that feels bigger than most.

The Athletic: 7 (Previous rank: 9)

From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall:

Reality check: The defense is still a problem

Detroit’s defensive EPA through eight weeks (minus-60.22) is the 16th-worst of any team in the last 10 years, according to TruMedia. Jahmyr Gibbs saved them Sunday by rushing for a career-best 99 yards after forcing a missed tackle, according to NextGenStats. He finished with 23 carries for 153 yards and now has more touchdowns in his first four seasons (59) than anyone other than Terrell Davis and LaDainian Tomlinson.

USA Today: 7 (Previous rank: 11)

From Nate Davis:

Does there need to be concern about RB Jahmyr Gibbs’ usage at some point? He’s on pace for 464 touches, which would be the second-highest total in NFL history. (James Wilder had 492 in 1984.)

Yahoo Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 10)

From Frank Schwab:

Biggest need: Defense, particularly at cornerback

The Lions’ fan base wasn’t happy when the Cowboys overpaid to get cornerback Joey Porter Jr. in a trade. They know that cornerback is an issue and it seems hard to believe the deadline will pass without Detroit doing something at the position.

Yet, there are other issues on a defense that has struggled most of the season, though it has allowed just 32 points the last two games. While the human element of linebacker Jack Campbell’s neck injury is overwhelming, and his recovery is the biggest part of that story, there is a football side to it as well. Detroit will presumably be without one of the best off-ball linebackers in the NFL indefinitely. While the team’s thoughts are primarily on their young star’s health, the Lions also have to deal with the reality of perhaps adding a linebacker before the deadline.

CBS Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 10)

From Pete Prisco:

They beat the Packers and the Vikings in consecutive weeks in low-scoring games. That’s a new formula for this team to win games, but a good sign.

ESPN: 9 (Previous rank: 11)

From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard:

Best in-season trade acquisition ever: DE Za’Darius Smith in 2024

The Lions have plenty of impactful offseason trades, including ones that helped them land quarterbacks in Jared Goff (2021) and Bobby Layne (1950). But the best in-season deal in terms of immediate impact likely goes to Smith. He had four sacks in eight regular-season games for the Lions, who had a team-record 15 wins and earned the NFC’s No. 1 seed in 2024. Detroit received Smith and a 2026 seventh-round draft selection from the Browns for a 2025 fifth-rounder and a 2026 sixth-rounder.

Sporting News: 11 (Previous rank: 12)

From Vinnie Iyer:

The Lions have come through with huge back-to-back home division wins against the Packers and Vikings. The big surprise is the improved defense. After allowing an average of almost 30 points in the first five games, the Lions have given up only 32 total the past two weeks. They should keep up that play with the Dolphins in Miami next.

item.title: The NFL has a quarterback problem. The Ravens just became Exhibit A
item.description: Baltimore's nightmare QB situation exposes a much bigger NFL problem: In a league built around elite quarterbacks, there simply aren't enough capable replacements to go around.
item.content:encoded:
The precise organizational term for the current state of the Baltimore Ravens is: screwed. It’s a fate that likely awaits every other team that doesn’t already have a quarterback succession plan in place, right this very moment. But Baltimore is uniquely beset by injury.

The Ravens lost all-everything quarterback Lamar Jackson on the very first play of Sunday’s game against the Bills to a thumb injury that could cost him the remainder of the season. Making matters infinitely worse, Baltimore subsequently lost backup Tyler Huntley to a toe injury that could cost him time. And time is not a luxury Baltimore has right now; the Ravens are scheduled to play the Jaguars on Thursday night. 

Oh, and just to add to the joy, undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, who leaped from emergency No. 3 quarterback into the lineup on Sunday, is himself dealing with an ankle injury. It rains, it pours, and sometimes, it Biblically floods. 

As for Baltimore’s quarterback options now, well … how’s your arm feeling? Can you get to Charm City by Thursday? 

The Ravens are in the teeth of the most vexing conundrum in the NFL right now: how to even survive, much less thrive, when your quarterback goes down. It’s the most important position in team sports, by a wide margin, and consequently the most challenging one to fill. More complex offenses, more ferocious defenses, more pressure and more expectation all combine to forge a few elite quarterbacks, and shatter the rest. 

You don’t need any kind of advanced metrics to know what your eyes tell you: there are more teams in the NFL than there are good quarterbacks to lead them. The numbers back this up: ESPN’s Total QBR stat, in this instance, is a useful benchmark. QBR doesn’t simply total up yardage and touchdown passes; it incorporates a range of game situations and quarterback attributes, making it a solid starting point for discussions of elite, serviceable and unusable quarterbacks. 

In the Total QBR system, a ranking of about 50 is average, and 25 is replacement-level. Players around the 50-point mark include Michael Penix Jr. (56.2), Sam Darnold (49.4) and Aaron Rodgers (49.2). So far, so good, right? At the low end of the 30 quarterbacks who have played enough to statistically qualify for the QBR leaderboard, you’ll find Jameis Winston (41.4), Deshaun Watson (40.9), Daniel Jones (39.4) and Justin Herbert (32.6) — again, no real surprises there. 

But when you look at the overall performance of all players who have taken snaps or thrown passes this season, that’s when you really get a sense of how bad quarterback play can be. Fagnano posted a QBR of 7.4 in his emergency stint on Sunday. Tanner McKee is at 30.7 after starting, and losing, three games for Philadelphia. And Cooper Rush posted an almost incomprehensibly bad QBR of 4.7 — again, 25 is replacement-level — in his two losing starts for Atlanta earlier this season. The Falcons might have been better off just direct-snapping to Bijan Robinson every play, and the Ravens might need to consider the same route with Derrick Henry. 

We can also determine the teams at most risk of a falloff due to quarterback injury by using a less scientific but more financially-motivated metric. Yahoo Sports’ Ben Fawkes has created a list of NFL starting quarterbacks’ value in terms of point spreads vs. their back-ups — in other words, the amount of value that a single starting quarterback brings to a team’s odds — and, again, the results won’t surprise you.

Per Fawkes’ metric, the quarterback most important to his team’s point spreads is — shocker — the Bills’ Josh Allen, who’s responsible alone for 7.23 points against the spread. Put another way, if Allen were injured and backup Kyle Allen needed to come in, any scenario where Buffalo was favored by fewer than +7.5 would immediately flip the Bills from huge favorite to pick-em status. That’s pretty damn significant! Wrap Josh Allen in bubble wrap, Buffalo! 

The next most important quarterbacks: Patrick Mahomes (backup: Justin Fields), Matthew Stafford (backup: Ty Simpson), and Drake Maye (backup: Tommy DeVito). Jackson comes in at fifth, responsible for 5.89 points against the spread, but that’s with Huntley as his backup. Now? The gap might be double digits.

So you can see the problem here. There already aren’t enough quality quarterbacks in the NFL, and the teams that have more than one in-house — looking at you, San Francisco — aren’t parting with them for anything less than obscene ransoms. 

Look upon the list of backups this year in the NFL, and despair. All due respect to Trey Lance, Quinn Ewers, Sam Howell, Davis Mills and the rest of the “hey, I remember that guy” guys holding tablets on sidelines across the league, but there’s just not much there there. 

The one hope that teams have is the Sam Darnold Scenario. Darnold, of course, sputtered from starter to backup, buried on San Francisco’s depth chart until Minnesota resurrected his career and Seattle cemented his legacy with a Super Bowl title. 

We have two extremely small sample size cases already this season: J.J. McCarthy, who seems rejuvenated with the Giants after flaming out in Minnesota, and Gardner Minshew, who checked in from 2019 to lead the Cardinals to a win over Dallas on Sunday. (McCarthy’s QBR this year is 60.5 and Minshew’s is 71.3, in case you were wondering.)  

Beyond that, teams have to either mortgage their future with draft capital — say, overpaying for Kirk Cousins, if the Raiders were even interested in trading him — or grit their teeth and weather the storm until the offseason. When demand for quarterbacks far outstrips the supply, it’s only a matter of time before someone — today, the Ravens; tomorrow, who knows? — ends up with nothing. That’s the reality in a league now centered on, and entirely dependent on, elite quarterbacks.

item.title: Caleb Williams has arrived as a top-tier quarterback
item.description: Make room for the Bears QB in the Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow club.
item.content:encoded:
In recent weeks, Simms and I have raised once or twice the question of whether Bears quarterback Caleb Williams belongs in the top tier of NFL franchise quarterbacks.

Based on Monday night's 34-point performance against a Seahawks defense that held the Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes to three points a week earlier, it's time to render a verdict.

Yes.

The new top four, in our view, are (in no particular order), Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Caleb Williams.

Lamar Jackson previously had been the fourth. A lost season due to multiple injuries puts him at No. 5, until he reestablishes himself in 2027. (And there's no reason to believe he won't, if he can get and stay healthy.)

For now, Caleb has crashed the party.

In Week 7 at Seattle, Mahomes completed 19 of 33 passes for 165 yards, no touchdowns, and one interception. His passer rating for the game was 58.9. In Week 8 at Seattle, Williams went 24 for 34 for 247 yards, one touchdown, and no picks. Williams also sparked a 39-yard gain on a key third-down backward pass to receiver Khalif Raymond, which set up the score that turned a 20-17 margin into a 27-17 clincher.

And before anyone says Mahomes didn't have any support in the running game, Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III and Bears running back D'Andre Swift averaged an identical 2.6 yards per carry against the Seahawks' defense.

So, yes, Caleb is a top-level NFL quarterback. Despite missing three games with a hamstring injury, his odds to win the NFL MVP award are down to 5-1, behind only Allen, Brock Purdy, and Burrow.

If the Bears keep doing what they did on Monday night — and if they finish the season with the No. 1 seed in the NFC — Williams will get plenty of votes. And he has a real chance to win it.

Even if he'd much rather win the MVP award not for the regular season, but for the Super Bowl.

item.title: The 49ers are reportedly ‘still looking for a receiver and a pass rusher’

item.content:encoded:
NFL insider Jordan Schultz told The Pivot podcast what to expect ahead of the NFL trade deadline. Unprompted, he brought up the San Francisco 49ers:

Last week, I talked about San Francisco and Chicago. Those were two teams that I thought would be really active. Now, the Bears landed [Jeffery] Simmons in a blockbuster. San Francisco got [DeForest] Buckner. So we were in on that.

But Ryan, I don’t think either team is done. I think the 49ers are still looking for a receiver and a pass rusher. I wouldn’t rule out another move for either team. There’s a lot of Khalil Mack buzz for both clubs. The Jets have made it clear they’re not looking to trade their stars, including Garrett Wilson. But there has been some curiousity around Breece Hall, so we’ll see what happens there.

Earlier in the segment, Schultz said these were the trade targets to watch:

Brian Thomas Jr. – Jaguars
Jauan Jennings – Vikings
Calvin Ridley – Titans
Jerry Jeudy – Browns
Kayshon Boutte – Texans
Hollywood Brown – Eagles

Schultz followed that up by saying, “But the biggest name around the league that people are really starting to get curious about is George Pickens in Dallas. He’s playing on the franchise tag. He has not been utilized the same way as last year. ”

The market for a pass rusher may not involve as many names as wide receiver. Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh recently said, “I want Khalil Mack here. Khalil Mack wants to be here. He’s one of the pillars of our team.”

The Jets have Will McDonald IV, who had a sack in Week 8, but can go long stretches without making an impact.

Arizona has a pass rusher in Josh Sweat who I believe teams will overpay for, if he’s moved at all. It’s hard to imagine the Cardinals going out of their way to make the 49ers better.

item.content:encoded:
The Daily Slop – 3 November 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Articles

Riggo’s Rag

Trey Amos gives Commanders a glimpse of something bigger than one win

The 2025 second-round pick out of Ole Miss had himself a ballgame, shutting down everything in his path. Amos also should have had his first career interception, but it was called back for a very dubious unnecessary roughness penalty on edge rusher K’Lavon Chaisson.

It’s exactly what Washington needed from a player many believe can be a franchise cornerstone.

With Amos, it’s all been about availability. His rookie season was cut short due to a fractured fibula, and an ankle injury sustained in his second practice of training camp delayed the defensive back’s 2026 debut until Week 6 at the San Francisco 49ers.

But whenever Amos has played, he’s produced.

He had six pass deflections as a rookie and two more on Sunday night, while allowing only one reception for seven yards.

When he’s been healthy, Amos has shown the potential to be a star. He has the instincts and measurables of a Pro Bowl-level lockdown corner who can provide stability at the position for years.

And even though he was out for almost a year, Amos has gotten back into his groove much quicker than anticipated.

It’s hard to overstate the difference Amos has made for Washington since his return.
