item.title: Some Long-Term Thoughts on the New York Jets at 2-6
item.description: How has the long-term view changed roughly half-way through?
item.content:encoded:
It may certainly be “Same Old Jets” vibes at 2-6, with another season seemingly over before we’ve even gotten through most of November. But while this team isn’t good, I do think it’s quite a bit different than the majority of the Jets teams we’ve seen over the last several years.

Some previous Jets teams have outright sucked and actually managed to win a few games they probably shouldn’t have. This one is losing games they likely should be winning based on how they played on the field. It doesn’t make it any less frustrating, but to me, there’s been a slight difference. Here are some broader takeaways I now have after nearly half the season is complete:

The Offense Has a Bright Future

Through nearly half the season, as crazy as it is to say about a 2-win team, this Jets offense is probably pacing to be one of the better Jets offenses of the last 15 years or so. Let’s take a look at where some prior Jets offenses ranked through eight weeks: 29th, 17th, 32nd, 30th, 26th, and 32nd. Being 12th in EPA/Play and 10th in Success Rate is an extreme upgrade over what we’ve become accustomed to watching.

Nearly any metric you choose to utilize paints this offense as, at worst, average. Even more depressingly, put this offense on some of the Jets teams in recent memory (in particular, the Saleh ones), and this Jets team would have been a legit playoff contender.

Sometimes teams in small samples can have misleading metrics or stats that aren’t indicative of future performance. In this offense’s case, I don’t think that’s true. I think there’s a pretty legitimate reason to be optimistic about the offense going forward.

Outside of Geno Smith yesterday, everyone who started on that offense is under contract next year. The average age of those guys was 23.8. That’s crazy young. And the majority of these guys, whether at the skill positions or on the offensive line, were early picks. This is the type of continuity the Jets have never really been able to establish on that side of the ball. At least not in recent memory.

Offenses are historically proven to be way more consistent than defenses year over year. Normally, it’s much more difficult to improve upon your offense than your defense, as Jets fans unfortunately know. There’s reason to believe what we’re seeing isn’t just some random stretch of good performances, either.

To me, it’s very believable that guys like Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper, Braelon Allen, Mason Taylor, and Kenyon Sadiq continue to improve. None of these guys have played a ton of football, and all had various traits that made them enticing as prospects.

Armand Membou, Joe Tippmann, and Olu Fashanu I’d consider all to be, at the very worst, average NFL starting offensive linemen. Membou in particular has been lights out since his struggles to start the year. To me, there’s enough glimpses, whether on tape or statistically, to show that almost all these guys are NFL-caliber starters.

The red-zone struggles are another story entirely, and to me, you need to look long and hard at the staff on this. It’s honestly hard to grasp how an offense can move the ball as consistently as this one does between the 20s and then struggle so much once it gets inside the red zone. Is it Reich? Is it Geno? Is it luck? I’m not quite sure. I’d love to see the correlation, but I have to think it’s pretty uncommon for an offense to perform this well between the 20s and be this bad once the field gets shorter.

Regardless, due to the long-term makeup of this roster, I think it’s very plausible that the supporting cast around the quarterback just gets better and better over these next few years. A lot of this will depend on who the young future QB is going to be, but overall, there’s a lot to like here.

The Record Might Be Slightly Misleading

I expect to get some blowback here. And to be fair, I would fully understand it. No one wants to hear it, especially when the team just let two games against mediocre to bad teams slip away, but the Jets are probably slightly unlucky to be 2-6 right now.

Looking at Net EPA/Play, the Jets are in an extremely similar tier to the Raiders, Texans, Giants, Panthers, and Ravens. All of those teams have better records than the Jets.

The main problem for the Jets? They’ve been losing almost every close game they’ve been in. They’ve now blown multiple fourth-quarter leads. They have lost a whopping four games this year in which they outperformed their opponent on a Success Rate basis.

This shows up in their record in one-score games. For example, The Jets are now 1-5 in one-score games. A team like the Giants? 1 loss in 5 one-score games. A 3-1-1 record. That’s a major difference.

Now, I don’t want to sit here and say the players and staff deserve ZERO blame for this. They obviously do, especially when we watch them fail to execute in critical situations, both in regard to clock management and on-field performance. But simply put, most metrics show this team probably should have a win or two more than they do based on how they’ve performed. Some of it is simply bad luck.

The Defense Needs Serious Attention

We talked positively about the offense. I think it’s a unit where we’re beginning to see high-pick investments start to turn things around. The defense, on the other hand, is a completely different story.

This defense is a mess. Top to bottom, I’m not sure this unit does one thing well. The secondary has now really begun to struggle after a strong start. The linebackers are inconsistent week over week. And the defensive front is reliant on a rookie to be a game-breaking talent despite playing only seven career games.

Many, if not most, of the free agent signings have been marginal upgrades at best, and looking forward, there are very, very few long-term pieces here. How many of these guys can you feel confident will be starters for the Jets 2-3 years from now on defense?

I think David Bailey is someone you can be confident about. T’Vondre Sweat also showed enough flashes where I think he’s going to be a nice long-term piece. AZ Thomas is young and has flashed a bit, but he’s been very up and down. Dane Belton has played really well, but his contract is expiring.

Bottom line is, there’s not much here at all. And not only are they bad overall, they’re particularly bad on 3rd down as well as in the red zone, another major contributor to them losing games. One interception in the last 24 games tells it all, to be honest.

This entire side of the ball needs serious attention in the offseason. There are a lot of assets and there will be a lot of opportunities to address it, but right now there are very few reasons to feel good about where this defense is headed.

Similar to last year, I think it’s pretty much over for this unit. I would be very surprised if this unit finishes anything better than a bottom-5 unit by year’s end. The level of competition is about to increase, and they simply do not have the talent currently to compete.

Special Teams Is an Underrated Problem

Special teams deserves some attention here, too. This unit stinks. After finishing #1 in DVOA last year, this unit has quickly joined the bottom tier of the league. It continued yesterday with them giving up a kickoff return for a touchdown.

When you consistently lose close games, special teams has to be part of the conversation. It’s an underrated reason why this team has the record it does.

Braelon Allen Is Becoming the Future

And then there’s Braelon Allen.

I think it’s getting more and more difficult to ignore how good he’s turning into. He’s 22 years old and is already 4th in Rushing Yards Over Expected (+133), 1st in percentage of runs over expected (53.2%), and 7th in Yards Per Carry.

He’s also 11th in Pass Block Grade and 4th in true pass sets. He blocks well, too, as shown in this video:

Breece Hall has been pretty clearly replaced as the starter as far as I’m concerned. I think there’s still value in keeping him around as the primary pass-catching back and change-of-pace option. There’s a story you can sell yourself on there, especially with something like a 70-30 split favoring Allen.

But Braelon, to me, is beginning to look like the more talented back. He’s younger, exhibits far better vision, and has tremendous balance. I think he’s turning into a really good NFL running back, and he should be the future at the position.

Geno Makes Sense as a Short-Term Option

One other thing I’d like to see is Geno getting a 1-year extension prior to the end of the year, assuming he doesn’t turn into a total pumpkin. Unless he wants to play for a team like Pittsburgh or Minnesota, something like 1-year, $15 million should be fair for both sides.

Even when the Jets draft a QB, I think Geno should likely be the Week 1 starter in 2027. There’s no reason to rush a young quarterback into a situation right away, especially if you have a capable starter on the roster, which Geno appears to be.

I Think This Coaching Staff Is Gone

I was unsure a couple of weeks ago. I thought at 2-4, there was a chance the Jets could win these next two games and sit at 4-4 with a whole different sentiment. Now? I think that’s over. I think this coaching staff is gone.

They just lost two very winnable games. Games that they arguably should have won based on how they played for stretches. Aaron Glenn continued his trend yesterday of making negative game-time decisions, and it hurt the team from a probability standpoint.

When you’re losing very close games, you need to really look into why. Where are the high-leverage swings happening? We talked about some of it being a result of the red-zone offense, defense, and special teams. But some of it is simply coaching and clock management. We don’t need to beat a dead horse here.

With the young offensive talent already here, I don’t really see the point in giving him three more first-round picks to use with all the question marks surrounding him.

I’m Still Optimistic for the Future

And to be honest, I’m more optimistic now than I was prior to the year. I do think it’s appropriate to have some positive feelings about where they sit. I get that no Jets fan wants to hear it with how bad the record is once again, but I actually think there’s a pretty solid foundation offensively.

The offensive line is more or less solid. The young pass catchers appear to be very solid as well. Braelon Allen is very much a good NFL running back. And the best part is that these guys are all young and under contract.

The cap space is finally recovered. The dead money is over. They’re going to have more assets than everyone. Right now, it looks very likely that two of these picks will be top 10 and the third might also be very high up. There’s zero reason this team can’t improve drastically in 12 months with all the assets they have and the current core on offense. I’m not sure I said that once over the past decade.

The defense and coaching staff are obviously major questions, and it’s going to be highly dependent on who they draft, but I don’t think the entire situation is as bleak as the 2-6 record makes it seem.

I’m more optimistic now due to the positive performances of this offense and some of the younger players than I was. We’ll see if I’m right.

item.title: Seahawks Droppings: Forget repeat, Seahawks might miss playoffs after faceplant vs. Bears
item.description: Seattle gets hammered by Chicago 34-17, playoff hopes dim.
item.content:encoded:
A little over a week ago, we were all riding high after Seattle dismantled the previously unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs. Within that span of time, the Seattle Seahawks also traded for a future Hall of Fame offensive guard and were finally ready to unleash their top two running backs. Things were looking rosy as they prepared to face the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football.

Then, the game kicked off. 

No sugarcoating it, Seattle sucked a big one tonight. The offense was horrible. The defense was gashed for the first time really all season. The special teams was putrid. All of that culminated in a 34-17 thrashing. Seattle is now 4-4 and all but out of the NFC West race already. Heck, they might not even make the playoffs at this point. They certainly didn’t look like a playoff team tonight.

Seahawks Droppings

  • If there was one positive, it was Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Chalk up another 100-yard receiving performance with a TD. Outside of JSN, there was nothing going on with the offense. 
  • Stupid, untimely penalties. Right when Seattle seemed like they were clawing back into the game, they would commit a dumb penalty. The main one I can think of is the Mike Morris one on the kickoff after the Seahawks made it a three point game. That field position helped the Bears extend their lead. 
  • The new offensive line looked like the old offensive line…maybe even worse. I figured there would be some growing pains with Charles Cross out, Quenton Nelson getting brought up to speed, and Grey Zabel moving to the right side. Sam Darnold and the running backs will be feeling those pains tomorrow. Darnold was under constant pressure the whole night, while there was zero room for the backs. It’s hard to do anything on offense when the line is getting manhandled. 
  • Bad Jason Myers strikes again. The missed PAT early on was bad juju when the offense finally got something going. Then, he had a chip shot FG blocked. Even the good special teams plays turned out poorly like when Seattle blocked a punt only to have it roll 45 yards. You can’t make that stuff up. 
  • Caleb Williams had way too much time. For the vast majority of the game, Williams was able to sit back and dissect the secondary. Even when Seattle did get some pressure, Williams routinely got out of it and made a play. Leonard Williams getting hurt certainly didn’t help things, but Seattle’s pass rush was nonexistent tonight. 
  • The energy was off. I’m not sure why Seattle seemed so flat tonight. Maybe the fact that this was their third primetime game in a row made it hard for the team to get their energy right? Whatever the reason, Chicago were the ones playing fast and aggressive, punching Seattle in the mouth. The Seahawks answer to that seemed to be “Thank you sir, may I have another?”
  • Darnold looked jittery. Part of that was due to him getting pressured early and often. Other times, he missed some wide open throws. And how many balls were batted down tonight? One of those resulted in an interception. I’m still not convinced that Schneider is completely sold on Darnold after this season. 
  • Seattle was outcoached. Offense, defense, special teams were all to blame. I can’t remember another time where I thought Mike Macdonald was so thoroughly outfoxed as he was tonight. Maybe the primetime game against the Lions in his first season? The red zone offense and defense continues to be a problem that is keeping this team from reaching its potential. Macdonald is still one of the best coaches in the league, but he has his work cut out for them to get the Seahawks back to contention. 

This game shows just how quickly things can turn in the NFL. Last week, Seattle looked like one of the best teams in the NFL, poised to make another run. In this game, they looked like a pretender who may not even make the playoffs. The pressure is off now. This is barely a playoff-caliber team let alone one who will compete for championships. It’s not time to totally jump the ship, but worrying about the division is a fool’s errand at this point.

item.title: Panthers vs Packers game review: Time to pivot
item.description: If things have to get worse before they can get better, the ‘get better’ part needs happen soon.
item.content:encoded:
The midway point of the NFL season is fast approaching, and the Carolina Panthers are not trending in the right direction. After 2 losses in 5 days, the magic ran out quickly and the plucky media darlings with an explosive offense have turned back into the pumpkin we all know and begrudgingly love.

With all the evidence of Ejiro Evero’s tenure as the Defensive Coordinator, another loss in embarrassing fashion was enough to force Dave Canales’ hand to go in a different direction. While Evero has plenty of supporters within league circles that sing his praises and tout his merit as a coach, the consistency of the the defense’s inconsistency wore too thin.

If there was ever a time to makes these changes it’s now, as despite everything, the Panthers are still in the lead for the NFC South title. As we all know, the NFC South counts as a division the same way that Thursday Night Football counts as primetime: barely. Anything can happen, and I’m not sure if that’s actually a good thing.

While many different areas of the Panthers flailing, it’s the defense that is in the most desperate need of some change. On Thursday, Packers quarterback Jordan Love dropped back 41 times. The Panthers did not register a single quaterback hit, let alone a sack. If they were playing drop 8 coverage the entire game, then fine. But no, they also blitzed 44% of the time, according to SumerSports.

According to NFL’s NextGenStats, Jordan Love had a 2.47 second time to throw. So maybe he was just getting the ball out quickly underneath? Well, Love had the 10th highest average completed air yards (6.4 yards) in the NFL and the 5th highest intended air yards (9.8 yards) during Week 8.

To the Panthers credit, they were able to hold the Packer’s to a pretty dismal rushing day. I’d like to give kudos, but I have a hard time reconciling that the Panthers had to sell out to stop the rushing attack of the league’s worst rushing team in order to find that success.

Granted, when you are among the league’s worst rushing defense, maybe that’s what is necessary. Maybe they do have to sell out to stop the run and everything else be damned regardless of opponent or circumstance? Who knows, but hopefully a new defensive coordinator can help figure it out.

If the Panthers do want to win the NFC South crown and make more than a whimper in the playoffs, it’s not going to happen if they stay as the defense ranked 28th in points per game, 22nd in yards per game, 30th in rush defense, 30th in pressure rate, 28th in 3rd down stop rate and dead last in the NFL in red zone stop rate. If you’re going to be bend-but-don’t-break, the ‘don’t break’ part is a crucial component.

Being 4th in takeaways is nice, at least. Hopefully that sticks around. I guess we’ll find something soon, when the Panthers take on the Denver Broncos. Until then, keep pounding.

item.title: Film study: Cade Mays is still the Detroit Lions’ best center
item.description: Cade Mays had a flawless start in second game for the Detroit Lions, cut short with an ankle injury
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions are 2-0 in the division and on a three-game win streak after ending the Minnesota Vikings’ undefeated start to the 2026 season. While the score only resulted in a 19-15 final, the Lions racked up 230 yards rushing against the NFL’s premier defensive unit.

Starting center Cade Mays entered the game in his second start of the season after suffering a fractured wrist in training camp. In his absence, backup Juice Scruggs had performed very well. Against Minnesota, Mays’ day was cut short after the first offensive possession in the second quarter, resulting in only 22 snaps played. Again, Scruggs filled in and played at a high level.

With Mays in the game, the Lions only rushed for 31 yards. With Scruggs, the team captured the remaining 199 yards on the ground in just under three quarters of play.

But correlation is not causation.

For this film study, I went back to watch the all-22 film of all 22 of Mays’ snaps against the Vikings. The quick conclusion is this: Mays did not lose a single rep of his one-on-one matchups in either the run or pass game. Despite the various looks, pre-snap shifts, and varied simulated blitzes, Mays’ day was about as flawless as you could ask for.

Below, I’ve clipped three plays that highlight the high-level play from Mays and capture the upside of what this offense can look like with him moving forward.

Athleticism and strength in the run game

The first play is an outside zone run play to the left. In the scheme, Mays is responsible for the gap to his left, but pre-snap there is no defender in the A-gap or even over the guard. The nearest defender is lined up in the B-gap as a 3-technique just outside of left guard Christian Mahogany. At the snap, the 3-technique defensive tackle stunts inside across Mahogany’s face and into Mays’ zone. Mays reaches the stunting defender, captures outside leverage by not stopping his feet at the point of contact, and continues to drive and strain through the whistle. The result: displacing the line of scrimmage for the soon-to-be MVP Jahmyr Gibbs to pick up a positive gain.

Anchor and strain in pass protection

The next play shown below highlights the size, strength, and finish Mays provides in the interior of the pocket for quarterback Jared Goff to rely on. At the snap, Mays absorbs and anchors against a strong bull rush from the defensive tackle, but once Goff steps up and the defender starts to swim out of his initial rush, Mays switches gears like a Ford F-150, driving his guy into the dirt once he gains leverage. If Goff had taken an extra moment to settle into the throw, the play could have resulted in Gibbs walking in for a touchdown.

Mental processing and physical adaptation

The final play highlighted below shows how Mays was able to mentally process the simulated pressure of the linebacker lined up as the 0-technique right over him and adjust when the blitz did not materialize. Not only does Mays make the initial recognition, but he is also able to adapt to pick up the presnap B-gap blitzing linebacker who stunts into the A-gap. From there, Mays picks up the defender and establishes leverage by moving his feet and hips to prevent the pocket from collapsing. The result is enough time for Goff to deliver the biggest explosive pass of the game, a 46-yard deep shot to Jameson Williams in stride.

The aim of this film study was not to put down or dismiss Scruggs’ performance, which was very strong in its own right. In fact, Dan Campbell was asked on 97.1 about Scruggs and whether his quality play has started a competition at the center position.

“… to get thrust back in there against that defense with everything that they were doing, to have that production, I mean, that was impressive. He was locked in. He was so ready to go. He was. I told you this before, we love Juice. He just fits us. He’s all about business, he’s a great teammate, he’s high-energy, he tries to finish plays, runs off the football. So he did a heck of a job.

As of right now, he’s our guy, because I don’t see Cade practicing Wednesday and he might not Thursday. So we’re going to get Juice ready to go here.”

At the end of the day, the Lions have two starting-caliber NFL centers on their roster. This is a huge credit to Brad Holmes for his effort in transforming the offensive line this offseason. The takeaway is clear, though. The ceiling for the Lions’ offense is highest with Cade Mays as the point man.

item.title: State of the NFC South: Week 8
item.description: Only one winner from the division puts first place fully up in the air.
item.content:encoded:
Only one winner from the NFC South this week, one on bye week, and one of the worst games of the season.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers:

So, let’s address that worst game of the season. With horrible weather in Tampa Bay, the Buccaneers shut out the Atlanta Falcons 16-0, and as you can guess, it was ugly. With this being between two NFC South teams, I’ll get to the Buccaneers’ defensive performance there and speak on how much trouble they gave Michael Penix, but let’s focus on Tampa Bay’s offense.

QB Baker Mayfield was, and I’m not joking, 0-3 on the day, and the Buccaneers had zero passing yards. If you had told me that statline, I would have thought it was a blizzard. The running game, obviously, was the star of the game. Bucky Irving had 170 rushing yards and 1 touchdown, while Kenneth Gainwell had 140 yards. Suddenly, Tampa Bay is on a two-game win streak, but their next opponent, the Chicago Bears, will be a challenge.

Carolina Panthers:

The other team that played this week was the Carolina Panthers, and after firing their defensive coordinator, they didn’t win. The Panthers are losing their lead in first place after going on a losing streak, but it wasn’t a horrible loss. Bryce Young played decently; the run game had a fine game, and the run defense did really well. The pass defense, which has been the issue this season, was what got exposed, but they did get an interception.

Carolina needs to break the loss streak before it’s too late, but their next game is against the Broncos.

Atlanta Falcons:

On the other side of that horrible game, the Falcons barely showed up. They attempted to pass, and it ended up with Michael Penix throwing 4, yes, 4, interceptions and only completing 8-24 passes. Then, when running the ball, they were seeing success but didn’t go to Bijan Robinson enough. The defense did their job, but the offense didn’t.

Maybe it will be better against the Cincinnati Bengals, but also, that team is 5-2.

New Orleans Saints:

The Saints were on their bye week.

It’ll be fun to see what changes the Saints make for their next game against the Cleveland Browns, because momentum must switch.

item.title: Patriots game ball: Who stood out in Week 8?
item.description: Drake Maye leads this week’s standout performers.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots are heading back to Foxborough with a win over the Miami Dolphins in hand, improving to 3-0 against their division and 5-3 overall this season. The game saw some standout performances on both sides of the ball and some solid overall football being played, mostly in the second half.

Who gets the Pats Pulpit game ball from the 24-19 victory, though? According to the community, it’s none other than the team’s starting quarterback himself.

Patriots game ball: QB Drake Maye

Community quote: “Given the lack of skill player starters, Drake was absolutely fantastic.” — Rocky Coast

Garnering 53.7% of the vote, the Patriots’ starting quarterback took home game ball honors this week. It’s his third out of five possible awards so far this season after he also was recognized by the community for his performance in Week 4 against the Bills and Week 5 versus the Raiders.

While there were some robust challengers — more on those in a second — Maye being the game ball recipient of the week comes as no surprise either. The third-year passer, after all, was magnificent while leading his team on a come-from-behind win in Miami. In the second half alone, he went 9-for-10 for 146 yards with two deep passing touchdowns to Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas from 43 and 48 yards out, respectively. He also scored himself when he made a nifty move on a zone read to take the ball into the end zone from two yards out.

On the day, he completed 16 of 20 pass attempts (80.0%) for 199 yards and those two touchdowns. He did only have eight rushing yards on five carries, but with the aforementioned touchdown part of the equation still finished in the 90th percentile for expected points added per play (+0.42). He also finished in the 93rd percentile in completion percentage above expectation (+14.0).

In a way, it was a typical day in the office for New England’s QB1. However, he also was very good considering the circumstances and challenging elements.

Maye was not the only player getting some love by the community, though. Running back Rhamondre Stevenson finished second in the fan vote (28.5%) after gaining 82 yards on 19 carries, and touching the ball four straight times — one onside kick recovery, one reception, two carries — to ice the game. Defensive tackle Cory Durden finished third (10.7%) after registering the first 1.5 sacks of his career and being a problem along the interior defensive line all game long.

Through eight weeks and five Patriots wins, the Pats Pulpit game ball winners are Drake Maye three times (Week 4, Week 5, Week 8) as well as Christian Gonzalez (Week 2) and the offensive line (Week 6) once each.

item.title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 8: Quarterback position in flux
item.description: Breaking down offensive and defensive snap counts from the Ravens’ Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills
item.content:encoded:
Offense
  • QB: Joe Fagnano 40, Tyler Huntley 10, Lamar Jackson 1
  • RB: Justice Hill 25, Derrick Henry 23, Rasheen Ali 1
  • WR: Zay Flowers 42, Rashod Bateman 39, Ja’Kobi Lane 33, Devontez Walker 8, LaJohntay Wester 6
  • TE: Mark Andrews 29, Matthew Hibner 21, Josh Cuevas 13, Nick Vannett 11
  • OL: Ronnie Stanley 51, John Simpson 51, Cam Jurgens 51, Andrew Vorhees 45, Roger Rosengarten 51, Chuma Edoga 6, Carson Vinson 2

Lamar Jackson’s much-awaited return lasted just one play before he suffered a thumb injury, which sidelined him for the rest of the game. Then, backup Tyler Huntley exited the game after 10 snaps with a toe injury, opening the door for No. 3 quarterback Joe Fagnano to play the final 40 offensive reps under center. In the backfield, Justice Hill’s 25 snaps slightly exceeded Derrick Henry’s total (23).

It was a surprising zero-catch day for Zay Flowers, who was targeted five times in 42 snaps. Rashod Bateman played three less snaps than Flowers and caught one pass, as did Ja’Kobi Lane (33 snaps). Since returning from injury, Lane has clearly assumed the No. 3 wide receiver role, relegating Devontez Walker to a reduced snap count (8 plays).

The snap breakdown at tight end was more of the same as well, with Mark Andrews leading the group in playing time (29 snaps). Matthew Hibner had zero catches again in 21 snaps, while Josh Cuevas caught one pass for 15 yards in only 13 snaps. Blocking tight end Nick Vannett recorded 11 reps on offense.

On the offensive line, Andrew Vorhees got the start at right guard over Emery Jones Jr. and played 45 snaps. The other five starters all played the entire game (51 snaps). Backups Chuma Edoga and Carson Vinson combined to play eight snaps between the two of them.

Defense
  • DL: Nnamdi Madubuike 56, Travis Jones 47, Broderick Washington 37, Calais Campbell 27, John Jenkins 26
  • EDGE: Trey Hendrickson 48, Mike Green 47, Zion Young 35, Ethan Burke 34
  • ILB: Roquan Smith 52, Trenton Simpson 52, Teddye Buchanan 44
  • CB: Nate Wiggins 53, Marlon Humphrey 46, Chidobe Awuzie 43, T.J. Tampa 22, Keyon Martin 20
  • S: Malaki Starks 77, Kyle Hamilton 78, K’Von Wallace 47, Keondre Jackson 12

The Ravens’ defense played 82 total snaps against the Bills as the offense had multiple turnovers and short drives, forcing them to get back on the field. As a result, several players saw elevated snap counts compared to previous weeks, such as defensive backs K’Von Wallace (47 snaps) and Chidobe Awuzie (43 snaps), and front seven players Ethan Burke (34 snaps) and Broderick Washington (37).

Nnamdi Madubuike once again paced the front seven in playing time with Travis Jones playing the second-most snaps behind him. Madubuike had a half-sack and two quarterback hits, which led the team. In his season-high 37 snaps, Washington corralled his first career interception. Campbell and Jenkins combined to play 53 snaps.

Trey Hendrickson and Mike Green were neck-and-neck in snaps at edge rusher, followed by Zion Young and Burke — who were also just one snap apart. Roquan Smith exited the game briefly with an injury but returned to play 52 total snaps, racking up 11 tackles, two pass breakups and a forced fumble. Teddye Buchanan saw his most action of the season with 44 snaps at linebacker.

At cornerback, T.J. Tampa returned from injury and played 22 snaps, jumping Keyon Martin slightly in playing time. Nate Wiggins matched his snap total from last week (53), while Awuzie almost tied Marlon Humphrey in plays. Malaki Starks and Kyle Hamilton were the only defensive players with greater than 56 snaps, nearly going the distance.

item.title: Falcons cut defenders Drake Jackson, Jared Ivey
item.description: Atlanta’s likely clearing space for a pair of returning defenders.
item.content:encoded:
After a tough day for the Falcons’ run defense, they’re shuffling the bottom of the roster.

Atlanta announced yesterday that it had cut ties with defensive lineman Jared Ivey and outside linebacker Drake Jackson. One or both could return to the practice squad, and my bet would be Ivey, given that the team prioritized picking him up off of waivers after roster cutdowns.

Ivey had appeared in seven games for Atlanta this year, moving around a bit and chipping in six pressures, a sack, six stops, and five tackles, per Pro Football Focus. Against the Bears in particular he was a bit of a menace as a pass rusher, but over the past two games he had struggled mightily as a run defender working against Christian McCaffrey, Kaelon Black, Bucky Irving, and Kenneth Gainwell. There’s evident talent here as a pass rusher and I think he’s better than the past two weeks in run support, so I don’t think the Falcons are planning on letting him go if another team doesn’t snap him up.

Jackson, meanwhile, played 20 snaps over two games in Atlanta and was inactive against the Buccaneers. He may well return, too, assuming the Falcons can and will make room for him.

Why the moves? I think Atlanta Journal-Constitution beat writer Daniel Flick has it right:

James Pearce Jr. is expected to be ready to go this week, just in time to harry Joe Burrow and the Bengals. Abdullah, meanwhile, was super effective as a pass rusher against the Saints in Week 4—the last time he suited up for Atlanta—and has been a solid run defender and special teamer throughout his career. Getting both of those players back would be a boost for this defense in a tough matchup.

If Ivey and Jackson aren’t back, we’ll wish them well, but I’m hoping we’ll see both land on the practice squad.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings Week 9 Roundup: Chiefs fall fast after two losses
item.description: Let’s see where Kansas City is ranked for Week 9 of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 8 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Denver Broncos in a pivotal game for the division and conference standings.

Let’s see how the national media reacted to itin this week’s sampling of power rankings:

ESPN: 6

(Down from 4)

Best in-season trade acquisition ever: WR Kadarius Toney in 2022

The Chiefs had one of the league’s best offenses in 2022 and still added Toney, acquiring him from the Giants for a 2023 third-round pick and a 2023 sixth-round pick. He wasn’t a major part of the offense, but he made contributing plays to help the Chiefs to the No. 1 seed in the postseason. The greatest game in Toney’s career was Super Bowl LVII, when he scored a touchdown and generated a pivotal 65-yard punt return in the second half to help the Chiefs complete their comeback victory. That punt return is the longest in Super Bowl history. — Nate Taylor

The Athletic: 5

(Down from 3)

Reality check: They’re bringing Justin Tucker back?

It feels inevitable after Harrison Butker missed another kick Sunday, this one a 54-yarder with 2:36 remaining that might have changed the complexion of the game. Butker, 31, has now missed six field goals this year and 11 in the last two years, and the Chiefs just added Tucker to the practice squad. Tucker, 36, hasn’t played since 2024 and served a 10-game suspension last year following allegations of sexual misconduct.

— Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

Pro Football Talk: 7

(Down from 5)

Can the Chiefs beat the best teams in the league?

— Mike Florio

CBSSports.com: 7

(Down from 4)

The explosive running game of the 5-0 start has gone away the past two weeks, both losses. See the correlation? They have to get Kenneth Walker going again.

— Pete Prisco

Yahoo! Sports: 7

(Down from 4)

Biggest need: Receiver, but don’t forget about offensive line

This is no surprise: The Chiefs still need help at receiver. Their offense has been built around Kenneth Walker III to good results, but it’s an incomplete unit. Rashee Rice is productive but not a dominant No. 1, Xavier Worthy hasn’t broken out and there’s not much else to speak of. Among the Chiefs’ wideouts, Rice has 243 yards, Worthy has 230, Tyquan Thornton has 219 but he’s on injured reserve and nobody else has more than 65. It’s a team that is a perfect candidate to try to turn around Brian Thomas Jr.’s career.

But the Chiefs also can’t ignore the offensive line. Guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched for the second time this season on Sunday. Offensive tackle Josh Simmons has been a problem and was put on IR. Receiver would be the more splashy move, but adding to the offensive line might be even more prudent.

— Frank Schwab

USA Today: 10

(Down from 6)

Of QB Patrick Mahomes’ 321 passing yards on Sunday at Denver, 72% went to his running backs and tight ends. Here’s hoping K.C. can find him a difference-making wideout ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

— Nate Davis

Sports Illustrated: 12

(Down from 6)

Guys. Guys. Guys. GUYS. Guys. It was a false start.

— Conor Orr

Sporting News: 6

(Down from 3)

Patrick Mahomes got back on track with his passing in Denver, timed with the return of Rashee Rice as his top wide receiver. Andy Reid can point to one big reason why the Chiefs lost to the Broncos. They had a season-high 11 penalties go against them, after having only 41 in the previous six games, the second-lowest total in the NFL.

— Vinnie Iyer

FOX Sports: 5

(Down from 3)

That was a decent bounce-back game from the Chiefs after they got pounded by the Seahawks. They were literally inches away from beating the Broncos. Two losses in a row isn’t great, nor is the fact that Kenneth Walker III and their rushing attack struggled again. But Patrick Mahomes is playing his best football since his 2022 MVP season. That’s going to be enough to keep the Chiefs in the Super Bowl hunt. And if they add a receiver before the trade deadline, they might be the AFC favorites.

Next game: vs. Jets (Sunday, 1 p.m. ET)

Stat To Know: The Chiefs are one of only two NFL teams to rank in the top five in both total offense and scoring defense. They rank fifth in both categories, averaging 383.1 yards per game and allowing 18.7 points per game.

— Ralph Vacchiano

item.title: NFC West Recap: Seahawks, Rams go opposite ways to .500
item.description: The 49ers spent the bye at 6-1 and welcomed back a familiar face while the rest of the NFC West try to keep up.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers didn’t play in Week 8 and still sit at 6-1 atop the NFC West. While they are on bye, the best thing could have happened: The Seahawks got embarrassed at home, dropping a game to the Chicago Bears and putting them 2.5 games back in the division race.

The 49ers may have been on bye, but they weren’t quiet. They brought back defensive tackle DeForest Buckner from the Indianapolis Colts for a 2027 fourth-round pick, six years after trading him away. He joins a beat-up defensive line that pressured Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. on just three of 34 dropbacks in the Week 7 loss. Help is on the way!

Seattle Seahawks (4-4)

So much for the Kansas City Chiefs momentum. The defending Super Bowl champions got pushed around on their own field on Monday Night Football, losing 34-17 to the Chicago Bears at Lumen Field.

Many may have seen a Bears victory. I don’t think anyone expected the Bears to blow this thing wide open in the fourth quarter, up by three points, and have the Seahawks do Seahawks things to bring them back. After a backbreaking Colston Loveland fumble, the Seahawks not only managed to score a touchdown, but also got a two-point conversion to be down by three points.

You know how these games go. Chicago was a bit shaky covering Jaxon Smith-Njigba—something I see lots of defenses do, and I just don’t get it. Chicago’s offense was humming sporadically, but it seemed like the Seahawks were waking up to win this one.

Then this happened:

That was enough to open the floodgates. Final score: 34-17 Bears.

Seattle got guard Quenton Nelson in a trade from the Indianapolis Colts, as well as running backs Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price returning from injury. Despite this, the running game still went nowhere. After Sam Darnold threw an interception late that he didn’t even seem to realize was a pick, you have to wonder if there’s a quarterback problem in Seattle.

Sure, Seattle is now 2.5 games back, and that’s great for 49ers fans. The bigger question is the Bears. Did they need to be that scary in embarrassing Seattle?

Los Angeles Rams (4-4)

With a 24-9 win over the Chargers, the Rams are 4-4. That’s right, they have Ram’d it to .500.

The Los Angeles Rams beat the winless Los Angeles Chargers 24-9 at SoFi Stadium in the battle for L.A. nobody asked for.

It wasn’t pretty. The Rams didn’t pick up a first down on their first five drives, and they haven’t scored a touchdown on an opening drive all season. They led a 0-7 team just 10-9 at halftime.

But this is the Chargers. While the Rams haven’t scored a touchdown on an opening drive all season, the Chargers haven’t won a game all season. That’s right, defense carries this one. Rams safety Quentin Lake and cornerback Trent McDuffie each picked off Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert, and the field goals were the only type of points the Chargers could muster. Running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum both combined for 129 yards rushing while getting a touchdown each.

Quarterback Matthew Stafford finished 17-of-25 for 157 yards passing and an interception. Not exactly the encore to an MVP season. As I said, this was mostly a defensive game and the Rams’ running backs.

So the Rams own Levi’s South SoFi Stadium and are also back to .500. Credit where credit is due.

Arizona Cardinals (3-5)

We don’t even need to recap this game; rather, we will just jump to 1:35 in the third quarter. Because that’s when Jacoby Brissett got benched for Gardner Minshew.

And that means Minshew Magic. Also known as the QB, a bad defense like the Cowboys didn’t prepare for. You may need some audio to read the rest of this—call it setting the mood. Don’t worry, I’m here to help. Open this song in another tab and then continue reading.

So, 1:35 in the third quarter. Starting there, Arizona scored four touchdowns in regulation and would have won outright if kicker Chad Ryland hadn’t missed an extra point. Instead, it went to overtime, where a field goal sealed a 33-30 win over the Dallas Cowboys.

It’s fair to note that overtime came with just over a minute left in the game. Minshew took the Cardinals down the field and scored. Had the Cardinals made the extra point, there would have been no overtime.

Between Brissett and Minshew, the split tells the story. Brissett went 10-of-23 for 119 yards passing and an interception in nearly three quarters. Minshew went 17-of-23 for 188 yards passing, and three touchdowns in less than two, and three of his incompletions were spikes to stop the clock. He even got Cardinals legend Larry Fitzgerald’s attention with throws like this:

Beyond Minshew saving the day, another fun stat brought up during the broadcast is the Cardinals’ record in AT&T Stadium: they are undefeated. Nothing much has changed.

Hey, the Cardinals might be an NFC West rival, but I’m sure most of the people reading this would rather the Cowboys lose than the Cardinals win. And that was an epic loss for the Cowboys—one for the ages.

Onto Week 9

The 49ers come off the bye to host the Las Vegas Raiders. Las Vegas went into Week 8 at 3-4 on a four-game skid, then visited the New York Jets. And they could have lost to the New York Jets. They wound up beating the New York Jets 38-33. Kirk Cousins hasn’t been traded yet, so that game should be a headache for the 49ers, as Cousins seems to have career days against them.

Seattle hosts Arizona at Lumen Field in the week’s only division game. The Seahawks won the first meeting and can’t afford another loss. The Cardinals are running high on Minshew, who has been named the starting quarterback. Hopefully they can forget they are the Cardinals for one more game.

The Rams head east to face the 2-4-1 Washington Commanders, who hosted the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday night. The Eagles have worse injury issues than the 49ers, it seems like, and got smacked on Sunday Night Football. It’s the NFC East, but the Commanders can be sneaky on offense. The 49ers are starting to pull away in a competitive division, but it isn’t over yet. Commanders, make us proud.

1st:San Francisco 49ers; Next: vs. Las Vegas Raiders
2nd:Seattle Seahawks; Next: vs. Arizona Cardinals
3rd:Los Angeles Rams; Next: at Washington Commanders
4th:Arizona Cardinals; Next: at Seattle Seahawks

item.content:encoded:
With several quarterbacks injured on their 53-man roster, the Ravens have brought in another.

Per Tom Pelissero of Netflix, Baltimore is signing Kedon Slovis to its 53-man roster off of Green Bay’s practice squad.

Slovis, 25, has a connection to the Ravens’ staff through quarterbacks coach Israel Woolfork. He was Slovis’ position coach last season with the Cardinals.

Slovis made his pro debut last season with Arizona, appearing in two games. He attempted only two passes.

On Baltimore’s 53-man roster, Lamar Jackson is out indefinitely with a right thumb injury, Tyler Huntley was a non-participant on the Monday injury report with a toe issue, and Joe Fagnano was limited on Monday’s report with an ankle injury.

The team added Austin Reed to the practice squad at that position on Monday.

Baltimore will be at home to play the Jaguars on Thursday night.

item.title: Green Bay Packers News: Matthew Golden is putting together a wild second season
item.description: You can’t say Golden’s second year has been boring.
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Golden is pretty much always open and usually he can do something about it.

That’s about as positive a spin as I can put on the Packers’ second-year wide receiver’s ongoing problems with drops. On the one hand, you have to be open a lot to have as many opportunities to drop passes as Golden has. On the other hand…man, that’s a lot of dropped passes.

Most, if not all, of the writers in the APC stable were still pretty high on Golden even after his disappointing rookie year, and I think we all figured he’d have something of a redemption tour this year. But this is about as strange a second year as you could imagine. Golden has been legitimately great at times, but his struggles with doing the most basic thing you can ask of a receiver would be funny if they weren’t so frustrating. You gotta catch the ball! That’s like 95% of the job, maybe more!

And it’s resulting in some unintentional comedy in the box score. Golden currently has 16 more targets than Christian Watson, but only one more catch. He’s 33 targets ahead of Tucker Kraft, but only eight catches ahead.

Again, he’s clearly getting open, it’s just he’s not doing as much with the opportunity as you’d like.

The good news is we’ve seen plenty of wide receivers figure out their drops. Davante Adams is everybody’s favorite example, but Christian Watson might be a better one, or at least a more contemporary one. He, too, had some early career bouts of the drops, but he’s mostly put that behind him. Well, mostly. He, too, has had some issues with drops this season.

At least it keeps things interesting. How boring would things be if your receivers simply always caught the ball?

item.title: Jack Campbell injury update: Lions coach says LB 'improving' after neck injury
item.description: Lions coach Dan Campbell gave a new update on LB Jack Campbell, who remains hospitalized with a neck injury, during a radio interview on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
item.content:encoded:
There haven't been many public updates on Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell's injury status so far. But what has been announced has largely been good news.

Most recently, Lions coach Dan Campbell said that Jack Campbell was "improving" during a Tuesday, Nov. 3, radio interview, though he did not share any additional specifics about the linebacker's condition.

Dan Campbell's latest update came after Detroit posted a statement to social media on Monday, Nov. 2 providing an update on Jack Campbell. The Lions coach cited the statement in his own press conference later that day, sharing a similarly general update of his own.

"Your prayers are working," Dan Campbell said. "Please continue to do that. We'll leave it at that, so continue to pray for him. But it is positive."

Jack Campbell sustained his scary-looking neck injury while making a tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson in the fourth quarter on Sunday, Nov. 1. He remained motionless on the ground after the hit, where he was attended to by training staff and medical personnel. The linebacker was eventually carted off the field and taken to a local Detroit hospital.

Here's everything we know so far about Campbell's post-injury outlook:

JACK CAMPBELL INJURY UPDATE: Lions share 'positive news' on LB after neck injury

Jack Campbell injury update

Dan Campbell provided another small update on Jack Campbell's status during a Tuesday, Nov. 3, radio appearance on 97.1 The Ticket.

"It's not easy because he's always going to be on our minds over here," Dan Campbell said of Jack Campbell, when addressing the Lions' preparation for Week 9. "The good news is he is improving."

The Lions coach made it clear he is providing his players with updates about Jack Campbell's status through the team's captains.

"I think the thought of him – knowing he's doing better, and I've kept the captains up to date, and they've let the other guys know its good news," Dan Campbell said, referencing how players were reacting to the situation. "I think that helps everybody just get a better handle on all this."

Campbell also added that he is trying to keep his players focused on their upcoming game against the Miami Dolphins, expressing concern that "bad things can happen" if players aren't able to be all-in on their gameday responsibilities.

"All we can do at this point is just continue to pray for Jack," Campbell said. "Put our thoughts on him when we have a minute, and on his family. And it's working, like I said. Because he's improving."

Dan Campbell's update mirrored the Lions' most recent injury update on their All-Pro linebacker, which came via a statement posted to social media on Monday, Nov. 2.

"Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital. Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time," the team said in its statement.

Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital. Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.

— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 2, 2026

The Lions' head coach provided some good news when he took the podium for his press conference later in the day on Nov. 2. While Campbell didn't share any details about his team's linebacker, he told reporters things were generally positive.

"It's positive," Dan Campbell said. "Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We'll leave it at that, so continue to pray for him. But it is positive."

Pressed for more information, Campbell said he couldn't share anything else. He added that he briefed the Lions' captains on the linebacker's latest status after the coach visited him in the hospital, and he said the team "knows what's going on."

"I got to go see him last night," Dan Campbell said. "It was good, it was positive. I got to see his parents, talk to his wife. You know, everybody's in good spirits. It's about the recovery. It's a small setback. That's the family. They're very positive, so that's good in that regard."

REGGIE BROWN: Ex-Lions LB reflects on life-altering injury after Jack Campbell hospitalized

What is Jack Campbell's condition?

The Lions have not provided a concrete update on Campbell’s exact condition. The team said the preliminary results are positive, which Dan Campbell echoed at his press conference on Monday, Nov. 2.

However, the exact nature of Campbell’s neck injury and whether he has movement in his extremities has not been shared.

What happened to Jack Campbell?

Campbell went down with a neck injury after tackling Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson in the fourth quarter.

He stayed down as the training staff and medical personnel surrounded him and the cart arrived. Campbell was loaded onto a backboard before the cart took him off the field.

Lions teammates took a knee and looked concerned as staff attended to him. Defensive end Aidan Hutchinsonwas in tears while the game was paused.

The Lions announced late Sunday night that Campbell was resting and was scheduled to remain in a local hospital overnight for continued evaluation and monitoring.

He was transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury after exiting the team's Week 8 win over the Vikings.

Head coach Dan Campbell didn't have an update on the linebacker after the game.

"Thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family," the coach said. "He's being taken care of. We don't have any new information."

JACK CAMPBELL: Lions All-Pro linebacker to remain in hospital after scary neck injury

Who is Jack Campbell?

Campbell is a linebacker for the Detroit Lions.

The 26-year-old is in his fourth NFL season, all with Detroit. The Lions drafted Campbell with the 18th overall pick in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft after he starred in college for the Iowa Hawkeyes.

A native of Cedar Falls, Iowa, Campbell broke out during his junior season with the Hawkeyes, totaling 143 tackles, two interceptions, two fumble recoveries and a sack in 2021. Returning for his senior season, Campbell was named an All-American in 2022 and received the Butkus Award as the top linebacker in college football.

He also received the William V. Campbell Trophy, also known as the "academic Heisman," in 2022 for being recognized as the college football player with the best combination of academics, leadership and on-field performance.

More: Jack Campbell is a Lions team captain. Here's why his teammates love him

Campbell slid right in as a key piece of the Lions' defense after arriving in the NFL. However, he didn't officially break out until his third season. Campbell recorded 176 total tackles, three forced fumbles and five sacks en route to being named a first-team All-Pro and earning his first Pro Bowl appearance last season.

On May 21, 2026, the Lions recognized Campbell's breakout with a four-year, $81 million extension.

Prior to his injury in Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season, Campbell hadn't missed a game in his four-year career.
